ADD.summary: Docker Compose uses a Compose file to define application services. The Compose CLI creates and starts those services, connecting them with networks and supporting persistent data through volumes.
ADD.explanation: Compose reads a YAML configuration that describes an application as services. It creates and starts those services, connects them with networks, and can provide persistent data with volumes. A project groups the resources for one application deployment.
ADD.syntax:
docker compose [OPTIONS] COMMAND
services:
  SERVICE_NAME:
    IMAGE_OR_BUILD_CONFIGURATION

example.title: A web service with Redis
example.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:5000"
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
  redis:
    image: redis:alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
example.explanation: This file defines a web service built from the local Dockerfile and a Redis service. Compose starts the web service after Redis passes its health check.

useCases.title: Local development
useCases.scenario: Define and run a multi-container application from one configuration.

useCases.title: Persistent storage
useCases.scenario: Keep application data after containers are replaced.

useCases.title: Environment-specific configuration
useCases.scenario: Use separate files to adapt one application for different environments.

interview.question: What problem does Docker Compose solve?
interview.answer: Compose uses a Compose file to describe services and their configuration. The Compose CLI then creates and starts the services from that model.
interview.followUp: What other resources can services use? Networks connect services, while volumes store and share persistent data.

interview.question: What is a service in Compose?
interview.answer: A service is an abstract application component. Compose can run one or more containers from the same image and configuration for that service.
interview.followUp: How do services communicate? They communicate through networks that provide routes between connected containers.

interview.question: How do `up`, `run`, and `start` differ?
interview.answer: `up` starts or restarts the services in the Compose file. `run` starts a one-off container for a named service and its required dependencies, while `start` only restarts existing stopped containers.
interview.followUp: When would `run` be useful? It is suitable for tests or administrative tasks such as changing data in a volume.

keyPoints: The normal configuration filename is `compose.yaml`; `compose.yml` and older `docker-compose` filenames remain supported.
Networks let containers belonging to connected services communicate with each other.
Volumes keep data separate from a container and allow services to store or share persistent data.
A project represents one deployment and groups its Compose-managed resources.
gotchas: When both supported default filenames exist, Compose uses `compose.yaml` instead of `compose.yml` or older names.
`start` does not create containers. Use `up` when the services have not been created yet.
`run` is for one-off tasks, not for starting the whole application stack.

ARG.summary: Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT sets a container's default executable. Use docker run --entrypoint to replace that executable when the container starts.
ARG.explanation: An entrypoint is the program Docker starts by default when a container runs. The image sets it with Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT. Use --entrypoint with docker run to replace it with another executable, such as a shell. Arguments after the image are passed to the selected entrypoint.

parameters.name: --entrypoint
parameters.description: Executable name or path to start instead of the image entrypoint.

parameters.name: IMAGE[:TAG|@DIGEST]
parameters.description: Image reference from which to create the container.

parameters.name: [COMMAND] [ARG...]
parameters.description: Optional command and arguments passed to the entrypoint.

ARG.returns: A running container that starts the selected executable.

example.title: Override an image entrypoint
example.code: docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/bash example/redis
example.explanation: Starts a container from the image and replaces its normal startup program with Bash.

useCases.title: Inspect a container
useCases.scenario: Start a debugging shell instead of the image's normal application.

useCases.title: Change startup behavior
useCases.scenario: Run a different executable without rebuilding the image.

useCases.title: Set runtime arguments
useCases.scenario: Pass custom arguments to an unchanged image entrypoint.

interview.question: What is a Docker image entrypoint, and how can you override it?
interview.answer: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that starts when the container runs. To replace it at runtime, use docker run --entrypoint followed by the executable path.
interview.followUp: What happens to arguments after the image? They are passed to the selected entrypoint as its arguments.

interview.question: How do you start a shell in an image with another default program?
interview.answer: Use the --entrypoint option with docker run. For example, docker run -it --entrypoint /bin/bash example/redis starts Bash instead of the image's normal program.
interview.followUp: Why might this be useful? It lets you inspect or troubleshoot a container by starting a shell instead of the usual application.

interview.question: What value does --entrypoint accept?
interview.answer: The runtime override takes a string that names or locates the executable. The executable must be available in the container for startup to succeed.
interview.followUp: How is this different from overriding CMD? A command supplied after the image can override the default CMD, while replacing ENTRYPOINT requires --entrypoint.

keyPoints: ENTRYPOINT selects the executable Docker starts when the container runs.
Set an image's default executable with the Dockerfile ENTRYPOINT instruction.
docker run --entrypoint accepts the executable's name or path.
Runtime replacement is useful when you need the container to start a different program.
When ENTRYPOINT remains unchanged, CMD or the runtime command becomes its arguments.
gotchas: The value must be the name or path of a binary. It is not a shell command line.
A positional command does not replace the entrypoint. Use --entrypoint explicitly.

Bind mount.summary: A bind mount shares a file or directory from the Docker host with a container. It is writable by default and is useful when container and host need to read or change the same files.
Bind mount.explanation: A bind mount attaches a file or directory from the Docker daemon host to a path inside a container. Both sides see the same data. Container writes change the host by default, while a read-only option blocks container writes. The mount can hide files already present at the container destination.

parameters.name: source / src
parameters.description: Host file or directory path. It may be absolute or relative.

parameters.name: destination / dst / target
parameters.description: Absolute path where the source is mounted in the container.

parameters.name: readonly / ro
parameters.description: Makes the container view read-only.

parameters.name: bind-recursive
parameters.description: Controls whether nested mounts are included and their access mode.

parameters.name: bind-create-src
parameters.description: Creates the source directory when it does not exist.

example.title: Read a host directory in a container
example.code: docker run --rm --mount type=bind,src="$(pwd)/config",dst=/etc/app,readonly alpine ls /etc/app
example.explanation: This mounts the host's config directory at /etc/app inside a temporary container. The container can read it but cannot change it.

useCases.title: Share source code
useCases.scenario: You edit source code on the host while a development container uses it.

useCases.title: Persist generated files
useCases.scenario: A container creates build output that must remain on the host.

useCases.title: Provide read-only configuration
useCases.scenario: A container reads a host configuration file without changing it.

interview.question: What is a bind mount?
interview.answer: A bind mount maps a host file or directory into a container path. The container and host access the same data, so container changes normally appear on the host.
interview.followUp: How would you stop the container from changing it? Add readonly or ro to the mount.

interview.question: How do you create a bind mount?
interview.answer: Use --mount type=bind,src=<host-path>,dst=<container-path>. The destination must be an absolute path. Docker generally prefers --mount because its options are explicit.
interview.followUp: What happens when the source path is absent? --mount normally fails; bind-create-src can create the source directory.

interview.question: When should you choose a bind mount instead of a volume?
interview.answer: Bind mounts use a host path chosen by the user and are useful for source code, build output, generated files, and configuration. Volumes are managed by Docker and are better for application-owned persistent data.
interview.followUp: Why can a bind-mounted container fail on another host? The required host directory structure may not exist there.

keyPoints: It shares a host file or directory with a container.
Common uses include sharing source code, build artifacts, generated files, and host configuration.
The default mount is writable, so container processes can change host files.
Prefer --mount when creating bind mounts because it clearly names options and supports more settings.
The container destination must be an absolute path.
Nested mounts are included by default; --mount can control this with bind-recursive.
gotchas: A mount hides existing files at the container destination. Recreate the container without the mount to reveal them.
With a remote daemon, the source path must exist on the daemon host, not on the machine running the Docker command.
The --mount form errors when the host source is missing unless bind-create-src is used. The -v form creates a directory instead.

Bridge network.summary: A Docker bridge network connects containers on the same Docker host through a software bridge. User-defined bridges provide name-based discovery, network isolation, and configurable settings; they are preferred over the default bridge.
Bridge network.explanation: A bridge network connects containers on the same Docker host through a software bridge. Docker gives connected containers addresses from the network subnet, allows same-network communication, and normally uses masquerading for outbound traffic. Containers on other networks are isolated unless a port is published.
Bridge network.syntax:
docker network create [OPTIONS] NETWORK
docker network connect NETWORK CONTAINER
docker network disconnect NETWORK CONTAINER
docker network rm NETWORK

parameters.name: NETWORK
parameters.description: The name of the user-defined network to create or manage.

parameters.name: CONTAINER
parameters.description: A container name or ID to connect to or disconnect from the network.

parameters.name: --opt OPTION=VALUE
parameters.description: Optional bridge driver settings, such as subnet, gateway, IPv6, or masquerading.

example.title: Create and use a user-defined bridge
example.code:
docker network create my-net
docker run -d --name db --network my-net nginx
docker run --rm --network my-net busybox ping -c 1 db
example.explanation: This creates a custom bridge network and starts a container on it. Another container can reach the first one by its name.

useCases.title: Connect application containers
useCases.scenario: An application has several containers on one Docker host.

useCases.title: Isolate application groups
useCases.scenario: Separate unrelated services so they cannot communicate by default.

useCases.title: Use container name discovery
useCases.scenario: A container needs a stable name for connecting to another container.

useCases.title: Create an IPv6 bridge
useCases.scenario: A container needs IPv6 networking on a custom Docker network.

interview.question: What is a Docker bridge network?
interview.answer: A bridge network is a software bridge on one Docker host. Containers on that network can communicate, while containers on other networks are isolated by default.
interview.followUp: How do containers reach the outside network? Docker normally uses IP masquerading, so external devices see the Docker host's address rather than the container's address.

interview.question: Why prefer a user-defined bridge over the default bridge?
interview.answer: A user-defined bridge gives containers automatic name and alias resolution. It also provides a separate network scope and lets containers connect or disconnect while they are running.
interview.followUp: Why is the default bridge less convenient? Containers normally communicate there by IP address only, unless the legacy link option is used.

interview.question: When is port publishing required?
interview.answer: Publishing forwards traffic from a host address and port to a container port. Containers on the same bridge can access each other's ports without publishing, but other networks and outside hosts need a published port.
interview.followUp: How can the default host address be changed? Set the bridge option `com.docker.network.bridge.host_binding_ipv4`; despite its name, it can accept an IPv6 address.

keyPoints: Each bridge network has an IPv4 subnet and may also have an IPv6 subnet. Connected containers receive addresses from these subnets.
Use a user-defined bridge for application groups. It gives better isolation and lets containers find one another by name or alias.
A running container can join or leave a user-defined bridge with Docker network commands.
Create a custom bridge with `docker network create`; advanced options can set the subnet, range, gateway, and other settings.
Enable IPv6 when creating a user-defined bridge with `--ipv6`. You can also provide an IPv6 subnet.
Publish a container port with `-p` or `--publish` when clients are on another network or outside Docker.
gotchas: Do not use the default bridge for production when a user-defined bridge can be used. The default network has weaker isolation and does not provide name-based container discovery.
Avoid connecting 1000 or more containers to one bridge network because communication can become unreliable.
An IPv4-only configuration cannot be removed from the built-in default bridge; use a user-defined network for IPv6-only operation.

Build cache.summary: Docker reuses build layers when their instructions and input files are unchanged. Improve reuse by ordering layers carefully, shrinking the build context, using bind or cache mounts, and sharing an external cache.
Build cache.explanation: Docker creates a cacheable layer for each Dockerfile instruction. If an instruction or a file it uses changes, that layer is rebuilt, and every later layer must run again. Arrange stable, expensive steps before frequently changing files, keep the build context small, and use mounts or a remote cache when useful.

parameters.name: --cache-to
parameters.description: Exports build cache to a specified location.

parameters.name: --cache-from
parameters.description: Specifies remote cache sources for the build.

Build cache.returns: A faster image build that reuses unchanged layers and may import or export cache data.

example.title: Reuse dependency and package caches
example.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json yarn.lock ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/yarn yarn install --production
COPY . .
CMD ["node", "./src/index.js"]
example.explanation: This copies dependency files before application files, so source changes can reuse the dependency layer. The cache mount keeps downloaded package data for later builds.

useCases.title: Speed up local development builds
useCases.scenario: A source-only change should not reinstall unchanged dependencies.

useCases.title: Share cache in CI/CD
useCases.scenario: Build agents are short-lived and do not retain local cache data.

useCases.title: Avoid storing temporary build input
useCases.scenario: Large source trees are needed only to produce a compiled artifact.

interview.question: How does Docker decide whether to reuse a build-cache layer?
interview.answer: Docker checks whether an instruction and the files it depends on match an earlier build. If they match, it reuses the cached layer; otherwise, it rebuilds that layer and all later layers.
interview.followUp: How would you reduce rebuild work after a source change? Put stable dependency installation before copying the rest of the source, and copy frequently changing files later.

interview.question: How can a Dockerfile use the cache more effectively?
interview.answer: Order stable, expensive steps before steps that change often. Keep the build context small, use bind mounts for temporary source input, and use cache mounts for package-manager data.
interview.followUp: When should source be mounted instead of copied? Mount it when it is only needed to create an artifact and should not become part of the image or cache.

interview.question: Why use an external build cache?
interview.answer: An external cache stores build-cache data at a remote location. Use --cache-to to export it and --cache-from to import it, which helps share cache across ephemeral CI builders and local builds.
interview.followUp: What is a registry-cache setup? Use a registry reference for both options; the build reads existing cache data and pushes updated cache data back to that reference.

keyPoints: Docker can reuse a layer when its instruction and dependent files are unchanged.
Put stable, expensive instructions before files or commands that change often.
A small build context sends less data and lowers the chance of unnecessary cache invalidation.
Use cache mounts to retain package downloads between builds, even when a layer is rebuilt.
External caches let different machines or CI runs reuse the same build-cache data.
gotchas: A cache miss affects every later instruction, so place frequently changing instructions after stable and expensive work.
A bind mount does not preserve files in the image or cache. Use COPY or ADD when files must remain in the final image.
Writable bind mounts only keep changes for the current RUN instruction.

BuildKit.summary: BuildKit is Docker's build backend. It makes builds faster by solving independent work in parallel, skipping unused work, and using precise content-based caching.
BuildKit.explanation: BuildKit is Docker's build backend. It turns build instructions into a dependency graph, runs independent work concurrently, reuses precise content-based cache entries, and can export that cache to a registry.
BuildKit.returns: A built container image and, when configured, reusable build cache.

example.title: Create a configured builder
example.code:
docker buildx create --use --bootstrap \
  --name mybuilder \
  --driver docker-container \
  --buildkitd-config /etc/buildkitd.toml

docker buildx build --load . -f - <<'EOF'
FROM alpine
RUN echo "hello world"
EOF
example.explanation: This creates a container-based builder with a BuildKit configuration, then builds an Alpine image and loads it into Docker.

useCases.title: Run independent work in parallel
useCases.scenario: Builds contain independent stages or commands.

useCases.title: Reuse changed-file and content-based cache
useCases.scenario: Builds run repeatedly on the same or similar source tree.

useCases.title: Share cache through a registry
useCases.scenario: Several machines or build jobs need the same cached layers.

useCases.title: Use a custom frontend or LLB
useCases.scenario: A build format needs features beyond standard Dockerfile instructions.

interview.question: What is BuildKit, and how can it improve build performance?
interview.answer: BuildKit is Docker's builder backend. Its graph solver can run independent build steps in parallel and remove steps that do not affect the final result.
interview.followUp: How does BuildKit improve repeated builds? It tracks changes to local source files and transfers only the changed files between invocations.

interview.question: What is LLB?
interview.answer: LLB means Low-Level Build. It is a binary format containing a content-addressable dependency graph for build operations, including features such as direct data mounts and nested invocation.
interview.followUp: How does LLB support caching? It tracks checksums for build graphs and content mounted into particular operations.

interview.question: What does a BuildKit frontend do?
interview.answer: A frontend accepts a human-readable build format and converts it into LLB. Dockerfile is one example of a format used with BuildKit.
interview.followUp: Why use a frontend version? Frontends can be distributed as images, so a build can target a specific version that supports its definition.

keyPoints: BuildKit improves build speed and features compared with Docker's older builder.
It can avoid running stages that do not contribute to the final image.
Independent stages can run at the same time.
Build cache data can be stored in a registry and reused by later builds on other hosts.
BuildKit is the default builder for Docker Desktop and Docker Engine.
gotchas: Linux containers have full support. Windows container builds are experimental.
Docker uses the legacy builder for Windows containers rather than BuildKit by default.

CMD.summary: docker run creates and starts a container from an image. You can set its command, entrypoint, environment, user, networking, and health-check settings.
CMD.explanation: Docker creates a container from an image and starts its main process. The image can provide an entrypoint and default command; arguments after the image can replace the default command, while an explicit --entrypoint can replace the entrypoint.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Options that configure the new container, such as its entrypoint, environment, or health check.

parameters.name: IMAGE[:TAG|@DIGEST]
parameters.description: The image reference used to create the container. It can include a tag or digest.

parameters.name: COMMAND
parameters.description: An optional command that runs in the container or replaces the image default command.

parameters.name: ARG...
parameters.description: Optional arguments passed to the command or entrypoint.

CMD.returns: Starts a container process created from the specified image. The command's output and exit behavior depend on the container process.

example.title: Run a short-lived container
example.code: docker run --rm --name demo alpine:3.20 echo "hello"
example.explanation: This creates a container from the Alpine image, runs echo, prints the result, and removes the container when it exits.

useCases.title: Run a temporary task
useCases.scenario: Run a command in an image for a short task and remove the container afterward.

useCases.title: Start an application container
useCases.scenario: Start an application with a chosen image tag and runtime settings.

useCases.title: Open a shell for debugging
useCases.scenario: Replace an image's normal startup program to inspect or debug the container.

useCases.title: Monitor container health
useCases.scenario: Set a command that reports whether a service is working.

interview.question: What is the basic form of docker run?
interview.answer: docker run needs an image reference. Its general form is docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE[:TAG|@DIGEST] [COMMAND] [ARG...]. The command and arguments are optional when the image already defines defaults.
interview.followUp: How can a caller choose an exact image version? Use a tag such as ubuntu:24.04 or an image digest.

interview.question: How do CMD and ENTRYPOINT differ?
interview.answer: CMD supplies default behavior for a container. Arguments supplied to docker run replace CMD, but the image's default ENTRYPOINT remains active. ENTRYPOINT can be replaced only with --entrypoint.
interview.followUp: What happens when both are present? CMD or the runtime command becomes arguments to ENTRYPOINT.

interview.question: How are container health checks configured?
interview.answer: A health check runs a command to report container health. docker run can set its command, interval, retries, start period, and start interval, or disable an image health check with --no-healthcheck.
interview.followUp: How can the result be viewed? docker ps displays health status, and docker inspect can show the health status and log.

keyPoints: A container runs as an isolated process with its own file system, network, and process tree.
docker run requires an image reference.
A missing image tag defaults to latest. Use a tag to select a specific image version.
Use --entrypoint with a binary name or path to replace the image's default entrypoint.
Unless the image or runtime configuration changes it, the container user defaults to root.
Container health appears in docker ps output.
gotchas: A command given after the image is added as arguments when the image has an entrypoint; it does not replace that entrypoint.
In Compose, command does not automatically use the image's Dockerfile shell. Use an explicit shell when the command needs shell features.
A Dockerfile can define only one effective CMD. If several appear, the last one wins.

Container.summary: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications from a YAML file. The file describes services and their networks, volumes, configs, and secrets.
Container.explanation: Compose reads a YAML file that describes services and their settings. It can connect services with networks, keep data in volumes, and provide files through configs or secrets. The `docker compose` command uses this model to create, start, inspect, and stop the application.

example.title: A small Compose application
example.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
  db:
    image: redis:latest
example.explanation: Save this as compose.yaml, then run `docker compose up`. Compose creates and starts both services.

useCases.title: Run a multi-service application
useCases.scenario: A frontend and backend need to run together with a database.

useCases.title: Keep persistent service data
useCases.scenario: An application needs data to remain after containers stop.

useCases.title: Connect services and provide configuration
useCases.scenario: Services need private communication or shared runtime files.

interview.question: What does Docker Compose define?
interview.answer: Compose uses a YAML file to define a multi-container application. The file describes services and can also define networks, volumes, configs, and secrets.
interview.followUp: How do services communicate? They communicate through networks declared in the Compose model.

interview.question: Which commands start and stop a Compose application?
interview.answer: Use `docker compose up` to create and start the services described in the Compose file. Use `docker compose down` to stop and remove running services.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect the current service state? Run `docker compose ps` to list services and their status.

interview.question: What are volumes and networks used for?
interview.answer: A volume provides persistent data for services. A network provides an IP route between connected service containers.
interview.followUp: What is the difference between a config and a secret? Both are mounted as files, but secrets are intended for sensitive data and use a separate platform-level concept.

keyPoints: Compose defines and runs applications made of multiple containers.
The usual configuration file is `compose.yaml`, and it follows the Compose Specification.
Use networks to let service containers communicate.
Use volumes for data that must persist or be shared.
Configs provide runtime configuration as mounted files.
gotchas: A service can run one or more containers from the same image and configuration.
Secrets are mounted as files, so they should be used for sensitive configuration.

COPY.summary: `COPY` puts files from the build host into a container image. Use it to include application code, dependencies, or binaries in the image.
COPY.explanation: The Dockerfile `COPY` instruction moves files from the build host into the image. Its source path is resolved from the build context, and its destination path is inside the image. It is commonly used to add dependency files and application source code before later build steps.

parameters.name: host-path
parameters.description: Path to a file or directory in the build context.

parameters.name: image-path
parameters.description: Destination path inside the image.

COPY.returns: A container image layer containing the copied files.

example.title: Copy files into an image
example.code:
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY . .
RUN yarn install --production
CMD ["node", "./src/index.js"]
example.explanation: This image starts with Node, copies the project files, installs production dependencies, and runs the application.

useCases.title: Include application files in the image
useCases.scenario: Building for production or CI

useCases.title: Add dependency manifests before a build command
useCases.scenario: Installing dependencies

useCases.title: Combine a copied application with a runtime volume
useCases.scenario: Local development

interview.question: What does Dockerfile `COPY` do?
interview.answer: `COPY` transfers files from the host into the image during the build. The first path is the host path, and the second is the path in the image.
interview.followUp: How can development changes appear without rebuilding? Use a Compose volume to provide host files at runtime.

interview.question: What does `COPY . .` mean?
interview.answer: `COPY . .` copies the project files from the build context into the image's current working directory. `WORKDIR` sets that directory before the copy.
interview.followUp: What determines the first dot's available files? The build context passed to the image build.

interview.question: When should code be copied into an image?
interview.answer: `COPY` is useful when the image must contain the application for another environment, such as production or CI. For code that changes during development, a volume can expose the host files instead.
interview.followUp: Can both be used? Yes. The volume can replace the copied directory contents while the container runs.

keyPoints: The instruction has a source path on the host and a destination path in the image.
Use `COPY` to place project files or other required files inside the built image.
A preceding `WORKDIR` sets the directory used for later copy destinations when a relative path is used.
Copy application source code and binaries when the image must carry them to another environment.
Copy dependency files separately when the build needs to install dependencies from them.
gotchas: The source path must be part of the build context. Files copied into the image do not automatically update when host files change; use a volume for live development changes.

depends_on.summary: The depends_on attribute controls the order in which Compose starts and removes services. Long syntax can also wait for a dependency to start, become healthy, or complete successfully.
depends_on.explanation: The depends_on attribute controls the startup and shutdown order between services. With long syntax, a service can wait until a dependency is healthy, has started, or has completed successfully.
depends_on.syntax:
services:
  dependent:
    depends_on:
      dependency:
        condition: service_healthy
        restart: true

parameters.name: depends_on
parameters.description: A list of dependency service names, or a map from service names to dependency settings.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: The condition that makes a dependency ready: service_started, service_healthy, or service_completed_successfully.

parameters.name: restart
parameters.description: Whether Compose restarts the service after an explicit update of its dependency.

example.title: Wait for a healthy dependency
example.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
  db:
    image: postgres:18
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
example.explanation: The database must pass its health check before Compose starts the web service.

useCases.title: Control service startup order
useCases.scenario: An application needs a database or cache before it starts.

useCases.title: Wait for service readiness
useCases.scenario: A client must wait until a database accepts connections.

useCases.title: Require successful completion
useCases.scenario: A one-time migration must finish before an application starts.

interview.question: What does depends_on do in Compose?
interview.answer: depends_on defines relationships between services. Compose starts dependency services before the service that uses them and removes them in dependency order.
interview.followUp: How can a service wait for a database to be ready? Add a healthcheck to the database and use condition: service_healthy in the dependent service's long-form depends_on entry.

interview.question: What is the difference between short and long syntax?
interview.answer: Short syntax lists dependency service names. It guarantees that those services have started, but it does not wait for them to become healthy.
interview.followUp: What happens if the database process starts before it can accept connections? A healthcheck can report readiness, and service_healthy delays the dependent service until that check passes.

interview.question: Which conditions can long-form depends_on use?
interview.answer: Long syntax supports conditions such as service_started, service_healthy, and service_completed_successfully. It can also set restart: true so Compose restarts a service after an explicit update of its dependency.
interview.followUp: Does restart: true cover every container restart? No. The documentation says it applies to explicit Compose operations, not automatic restarts after a container dies.

keyPoints: Use depends_on when service startup or shutdown order affects how the application works.
A dependent service starts only after its listed dependency services have started.
The service_healthy condition makes Compose wait for a dependency healthcheck to pass.
The long syntax restart option lets Compose restart a service after an explicit update to its dependency.
gotchas: Short syntax only waits for the dependency container to start. Use long syntax with service_healthy when the application needs the dependency to accept connections.

Distroless image.summary: A distroless image is a minimal container image that includes an application and its runtime dependencies but omits most operating-system tools. This reduces the attack surface, image size, and startup time.
Distroless image.explanation: A distroless image is a small container image with the application, its runtime dependencies, and required metadata. It leaves out common operating-system tools, shells, package managers, and debugging utilities, which reduces the runtime surface and limits actions after a compromise.
Distroless image.syntax:
FROM <builder-image> AS build
# build the application
FROM <minimal-runtime-image>
COPY --from=build <runtime-files> <destination>
CMD ["<application>"]

example.title: A small distroless Python image
example.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --target=/out -r requirements.txt
COPY app.py /src/app.py

FROM gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian12
COPY --from=build /out /site-packages
COPY --from=build /src/app.py /app.py
ENV PYTHONPATH=/site-packages
CMD ["/app.py"]
example.explanation: This example uses a multi-stage build. Build tools and dependency installation stay in the first stage. The final stage contains the application and its runtime dependencies.

useCases.title: Run applications with fewer unused runtime components.
useCases.scenario: Production services

useCases.title: Use multi-stage builds so CI produces a small runtime image.
useCases.scenario: Automated delivery

useCases.title: Limit available tools and reduce the exposed runtime surface.
useCases.scenario: Security-focused deployments

interview.question: What is a distroless image?
interview.answer: A distroless image contains the application, its runtime dependencies, and required configuration or metadata. It normally omits operating-system tools, shells, package managers, and debugging utilities.
interview.followUp: Why can this improve security? Fewer components create fewer possible vulnerable parts, and the missing shell and package manager limit actions after a compromise.

interview.question: How should a minimal image be built?
interview.answer: Use a multi-stage Dockerfile. Put compilation and dependency installation in a build stage, then copy only the files needed at runtime into the final image.
interview.followUp: How should its behavior be checked? Use automated CI tests rather than relying on interactive inspection of the final container.

interview.question: What are the main benefits of minimal images?
interview.answer: Minimal images can reduce image size, vulnerability exposure, and pull and startup time. They can also make compliance work easier by keeping the runtime contents focused.
interview.followUp: Does minimal mean vulnerability-free? No. The image still needs continuous CVE monitoring, including with Docker Scout.

keyPoints: “Minimal image” and “distroless image” describe the same general approach: remove components that the application does not need.
The application itself is part of the runtime image.
The image must include dependencies required by the application, such as a C library or language runtime.
Removing unused components can reduce the number of vulnerable parts exposed in the image.
A smaller image usually takes less time to download and start.
Without a shell or package manager, post-compromise actions are more restricted.
Keep build dependencies out of the production image by separating the build and runtime stages.
gotchas: Do not assume common commands such as ls, ps, cat, sh, bash, apt, apk, curl, wget, or strace are available. Interactive inspection may not work, so test the image in CI instead.
A minimal image can still contain vulnerabilities. Continue monitoring it with Docker Scout.

docker build.explanation: The `docker build` command uses Buildx to send a build request to BuildKit. BuildKit reads the Dockerfile, runs its steps, and returns the image or sends the result to a registry. The final argument is the build context, such as the current directory.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Build options, such as `--tag`, `--file`, `--build-arg`, `--platform`, and `--no-cache`.

parameters.name: PATH | URL | -
parameters.description: The files and directories available to the build. Use `.` for the current directory, or provide a URL or `-`.

docker build.returns: Creates a Docker image. The output is returned to the client or uploaded to a registry.

example.title: Build an image
example.code: docker build -t my-app .
example.explanation: This builds an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory and gives it the name `my-app`.

interview.question: What does `docker build` do?
interview.answer: `docker build` is the command used to create an image from a Dockerfile. It uses Buildx as the client and BuildKit as the builder by default.
interview.followUp: What happens after the client sends the request? BuildKit resolves the Dockerfile instructions and executes the build steps.

interview.question: What is a build context?
interview.answer: The build context is the positional argument after the options, such as `.`. It supplies files that the build can use.
interview.followUp: How can the context be reduced? Add a `.dockerignore` file to exclude files that the build does not need.

interview.question: What are Buildx and BuildKit?
interview.answer: Buildx is the command-line client and user interface. BuildKit is the server process that performs the build workload.
interview.followUp: What else can Buildx manage? It can create and manage builders, handle registry image features, and run builds concurrently.

keyPoints: Buildx is the command-line client for starting and managing builds.
BuildKit is the builder that executes the instructions and build steps.
A build can return its output to the client or upload it to a registry such as Docker Hub.
`docker build` is a wrapper that passes build options to Buildx.
Docker Desktop and Docker Engine include Buildx and BuildKit by default.
With BuildKit, leading relative path components that go outside the context are stripped.
gotchas: The command normally uses Buildx and BuildKit. Windows container mode and `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0` are exceptions.
Use `.dockerignore` to keep unnecessary files out of the build context.
The final path or URL is the build context. It controls which files are available to the build.

docker buildx build.summary: Starts a Docker image build with BuildKit. It accepts a build context and options for files, tags, arguments, platforms, cache, and output.
docker buildx build.explanation: Buildx is the Docker CLI client for BuildKit. The command sends the Dockerfile, build arguments, export settings, and cache settings to a BuildKit builder, which runs the build steps and returns or exports the result.

parameters.name: OPTIONS

parameters.name: PATH
parameters.description: A local build context directory or another supported source.

parameters.name: URL
parameters.description: A remote build context source.
Read the build context from standard input.

docker buildx build.returns: The build result is sent to the client or exported to a configured destination, such as a registry or local Docker image store.

example.title: Build and load an image
example.code: docker buildx build -t myapp:latest --load .
example.explanation: Builds the Dockerfile in the current directory, tags the result, and loads the image into the local Docker image store.

useCases.scenario: Check Dockerfile build rules before running the build.

useCases.title: Choose a target platform

interview.question: What is the relationship between Buildx and BuildKit?
interview.answer: Buildx is the CLI client, while BuildKit is the builder that executes the work. Buildx sends the build request and displays progress.
interview.followUp: What does the request contain? It can include the Dockerfile, build arguments, export options, and caching options.

interview.question: What is the syntax of `docker buildx build`?
interview.answer: The command is `docker buildx build [OPTIONS] PATH | URL | -`. The final argument supplies the build context, which can be a path, URL, or standard input.
interview.followUp: How can you choose a different Dockerfile? Add `-f` or `--file` with its filename.

interview.question: How do external build caches work?
interview.answer: `--cache-from` imports cache from an external source, while `--cache-to` exports cache to an external destination. Supported examples include registry, local, inline, GitHub Actions, S3, and Azure Blob storage.
interview.followUp: Why use an external cache? It lets later builds reuse cache that is stored outside the current builder.

keyPoints: Use `docker buildx build` to start a BuildKit build.
Buildx is the client interface for starting and managing Docker builds.
BuildKit performs the actual build steps as the builder backend.
Build requests can include the Dockerfile, build arguments, output settings, and cache settings.
Use `--cache-from` to import reusable build cache from an external source.
Use `--cache-to` to save build cache outside the current builder.
gotchas: The build uses BuildKit, so a configured BuildKit builder must be available.
Use --check to validate the build configuration without running the build.

Docker Compose.summary: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications from one YAML file. It manages services, networks, volumes, startup, logs, and other application lifecycle tasks.
Docker Compose.explanation: Compose reads a YAML file that describes services and their settings. It creates the needed containers, network, and volumes, then manages the application together. Services can use images or images built from Dockerfiles. Compose also supports health checks, live file updates, persistent volumes, logs, and commands inside running containers.

example.title: A Compose application
example.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:5000"
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
  redis:
    image: redis:alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
volumes:
  redis-data:
example.explanation: This file builds a web service, starts Redis, waits for Redis to pass its health check, and keeps Redis data in a named volume.

useCases.scenario: Run a web application with a database or cache.

useCases.title: Persistent application data
useCases.scenario: Keep database or Redis data after containers are replaced.

useCases.title: Live development updates
useCases.scenario: Apply source changes while developing.

useCases.title: Debugging a stack
useCases.scenario: Inspect configuration, logs, or a running service.

interview.question: What problem does Docker Compose solve?
interview.answer: Compose defines multiple services and their configuration in one YAML file. A single `docker compose up` command creates and starts the application services together.
interview.followUp: How does Compose apply a file change? Run `docker compose up` again; Compose compares the declared state with the current state and applies the needed changes.

interview.question: What is the difference between a Dockerfile and a Compose file?
interview.answer: A Dockerfile contains instructions for building an image. A Compose file describes the running services and can refer to a Dockerfile through a service's `build` setting.
interview.followUp: Can a service avoid a local Dockerfile? Yes. The Redis service in the tutorial uses the public `redis:alpine` image instead.

interview.question: How can Compose prevent a service startup race?
interview.answer: A health check runs a command inside a service to test readiness. With `depends_on` and `condition: service_healthy`, Compose waits for Redis to become healthy before starting the web service.
interview.followUp: What happens if the check keeps failing? The configured interval, timeout, retries, and start period determine when Compose marks the service unhealthy.

keyPoints: Compose describes an application made from several containers.
One YAML file can define services, networks, and volumes for the stack.
`docker compose up` creates and starts the declared services.
Compose Watch can update a running container when project files change.
Use `docker compose config` to inspect the resolved configuration without starting containers.
gotchas: Data stored only in a container is lost when that container is removed. Use a named volume for data that must survive.
Starting services together does not guarantee that a dependency is ready. Add a health check and use a healthy dependency condition.
Do not use `docker compose down -v` when you need to keep volume data.

docker compose build.summary: Builds or rebuilds Docker images for Compose services. You can build all services or name specific services, and options control caching, pulling, pushing, attestations, and dependencies.
docker compose build.explanation: Compose reads the selected service definitions and builds their images from the configured source. A service can use a short build path or a detailed build definition, and the path is resolved relative to the Compose file when it is not absolute.

parameters.name: SERVICE...
parameters.description: Optional service names to build. If omitted, the command operates on the Compose application's services.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Options such as `--build-arg`, `--no-cache`, `--pull`, `--push`, `--quiet`, and `--with-dependencies`.

docker compose build.returns: Built service images, optionally pushed when `--push` is used.

example.title: Build and start one service
example.code:
docker compose build web

docker compose up -d web
example.explanation: Builds the image for the `web` service, then starts that service in the background.

useCases.title: Build and push images

interview.question: What does `docker compose build` do?
interview.answer: The command builds or rebuilds service images. Without service names, it processes the services defined in the Compose application; adding names limits the build to those services.
interview.followUp: How can a service's image receive a specific tag? Define an `image` name for the service; Compose uses that name after variable substitution.

interview.question: What can the `build` field contain?
interview.answer: A short `build` value is a context directory. Compose uses the directory as the Docker build context and looks for a Dockerfile at its root.
interview.followUp: How do you use a different Dockerfile? Use the detailed build form and set its Dockerfile location.

interview.question: Which options change what gets built?
interview.answer: `--with-dependencies` also builds the selected services' dependencies, including dependencies found transitively. `--no-cache` disables the image build cache.
interview.followUp: How can you ask for a newer base image? Use `--pull` to always attempt to pull a newer image version.

keyPoints: After a build, Compose tags the service image using a project-and-service name unless another image name is configured.
Use `--build-arg` to pass values available while the service image is being built.
Use `--no-cache` when the build must run without previously cached layers.
Use `--push` to send the built service images to a registry.
Use `--with-dependencies` to build service dependencies as well as the selected services.
gotchas: An absolute build path makes the Compose file less portable and causes a warning.
Rebuild after changing the Dockerfile or files in the build directory.
The `--memory` option is not supported when BuildKit is used.

docker compose down.summary: Stops Compose services and removes their containers and project networks. Optional flags remove volumes, images, orphan containers, or change the shutdown timeout.
docker compose down.explanation: Compose stops the selected services and removes the containers and networks created by `docker compose up`. Add `--volumes` to remove declared named volumes and attached anonymous volumes. Add `--remove-orphans` to remove containers for services no longer in the Compose file.

parameters.description: Remove containers for services not defined in the Compose file.

parameters.name: --rmi
parameters.description: Remove service images. `local` removes only images without a custom tag; `all` removes all used images.

parameters.name: -t, --timeout
parameters.description: Set the shutdown timeout in seconds.

parameters.name: -v, --volumes
parameters.description: Remove declared named volumes and attached anonymous volumes.

parameters.name: SERVICES
parameters.description: Limit the operation to the named services.

docker compose down.returns: Stops and removes the selected Compose services and their removable containers and networks. Optional flags also remove images, volumes, or orphan containers.

example.title: Remove a Compose application and its data
example.code: docker compose down --volumes --remove-orphans
example.explanation: Stops the Compose application and removes its containers, networks, named volumes, anonymous volumes, and orphan containers.

interview.question: What does `docker compose down` remove by default?
interview.answer: It stops the Compose containers and removes those containers and the project networks created by `up`. The default network is also removed when the project uses one.
interview.followUp: What happens to external networks? They are kept; Compose never removes networks marked as external.

interview.question: How do you remove Compose volumes?
interview.answer: The `--volumes` option removes named volumes declared in the Compose file and anonymous volumes attached to containers. It also removes the normal containers and networks.
interview.followUp: Why might a later `up` lose application data? Removing a named volume deletes the data stored in it.

interview.question: How do you remove orphan containers?
interview.answer: Use `--remove-orphans`. It removes containers for services that are not defined in the current Compose file.
interview.followUp: What is a safer alternative when an orphan may contain useful data? Inspect the container first instead of deleting it automatically.

keyPoints: The command tears down resources created by `docker compose up`.
Without extra options, it removes containers for services in the Compose file.
It removes project networks declared by the Compose configuration.
The generated default network is removed when the application uses it.
Use `--rmi local` or `--rmi all` to remove service images.
Use `--timeout` or `-t` to set how long shutdown may take.
Failed `pre_start` hook containers are cleaned up during teardown.
gotchas: By default, anonymous volumes stay after the command. They are not automatically mounted by a later `up` because they do not have stable names.
External networks and volumes are not deleted by this command.
Use `--volumes` only when the stored data is no longer needed. The deletion cannot be undone.

interview.question: What does docker compose exec do?
interview.answer: It runs a command inside a container that belongs to a Compose service. The container must already be running; this command does not start a new one.
interview.followUp: How would you run the command in a background process? Use --detach.

interview.question: What happens with TTY and interactive input by default?
interview.answer: It allocates a TTY and uses interactive mode by default. This makes commands such as opening a shell convenient.
interview.followUp: How can a script avoid terminal allocation? Pass --no-tty, and disable interactive mode when required.

interview.question: How do you target a particular replica and execution context?

interview.followUp: How can you provide values only for this command? Use one or more --env options.

interview.answer: docker compose logs displays log output from Compose services. You can pass service names to limit the output to those services.
interview.followUp: How do you watch new output from one service? Add -f or --follow and provide the service name.

interview.answer: It lists containers for a Compose project, including their current status and exposed ports. Without extra options, only running containers appear.

useCases.title: Control attached output
useCases.scenario: Limit attached output when some services produce too many logs.

useCases.title: Update services
useCases.scenario: Apply a changed image or service configuration to existing containers.

interview.question: What does `docker compose up` do?
interview.answer: It builds or pulls what the services need, creates or recreates containers, starts services, and attaches to their combined output. Linked services are also started when needed.
interview.followUp: How can you keep the services running after the command returns? Use `docker compose up --detach` or `docker compose up -d`.

interview.question: What is the difference between attached and detached mode?
interview.answer: By default, the command attaches to container output and stops the containers when it exits. Detached mode starts them in the background and leaves them running.
interview.followUp: How can you watch output after starting in detached mode? Run `docker compose logs -f`, optionally followed by a service name.

interview.question: When does Compose recreate containers?
interview.answer: Compose recreates a service when its configuration or image changed after the container was created. `--no-recreate` disables this behavior, while `--force-recreate` recreates all containers.
interview.followUp: What happens to mounted volumes during recreation? Compose preserves mounted volumes, but removing named volumes with `down -v` deletes their stored data.

keyPoints: The command can build images, create containers, start them, and attach your terminal to their output.
Required linked services start too unless they are already running.
Use `--attach` to limit which services produce attached output.
Use `--no-attach` to exclude noisy services from attached output.
A command error returns exit code 1.
Interrupting the command stops the containers and returns exit code 0.
gotchas: Without detached mode, ending the attached command stops the containers.
Use --no-recreate when existing containers must not be replaced because of configuration or image changes.
Removing named volumes permanently deletes the data stored in them.

docker context.summary: Docker contexts let one Docker CLI manage different Docker daemons. Select a context to choose the daemon targeted by Docker commands.
docker context.explanation: A Docker context stores the information the Docker CLI needs to manage a daemon, such as its name, endpoint, and TLS data. Use context commands to create, inspect, list, update, export, import, remove, or select contexts. The selected context controls where Docker commands run unless a command flag or environment variable overrides it.
docker context.syntax:
docker context <subcommand>
docker context use CONTEXT
docker --context CONTEXT <command>
DOCKER_CONTEXT=CONTEXT

parameters.name: CONTEXT
parameters.description: The context name to create, select, inspect, update, export, import, or remove.

parameters.name: host endpoint
parameters.description: The Docker daemon endpoint used by a context, such as tcp://docker:2375.

parameters.name: context file
parameters.description: A file containing an exported context for import.

docker context.returns: Commands print context names or status messages. docker context ls lists contexts; docker context inspect displays detailed context data; docker context show prints the current context name.

example.title: Create and switch contexts
example.code:
docker context create staging --docker host=tcp://docker.example:2375
docker context use staging
docker ps
docker context use default
example.explanation: Creates a context, makes it active, runs a command against its Docker daemon, and switches back.

useCases.title: Switch between daemons
useCases.scenario: Manage local and remote Docker daemons from one client.

useCases.title: Use a temporary context

useCases.title: Export and import a context
useCases.scenario: Copy daemon connection settings to another host.
