useCases.scenario: Check or change endpoint and description settings.

interview.question: What is a Docker context?
interview.answer: A context is a group of Docker daemon settings, including an endpoint and TLS information. It lets one Docker client manage different daemons.
interview.followUp: How can you check which context is active? Run docker context show, or look for the asterisk in docker context ls.

interview.question: How do you change the context used by Docker commands?
interview.answer: Use docker context use CONTEXT to save the default context. For a one-time command, use docker --context CONTEXT COMMAND instead.
interview.followUp: How can you select a context only for the current shell? Set DOCKER_CONTEXT; it overrides the saved default until you unset it.

interview.question: How do you move a context to another host?
interview.answer: Use docker context export to write a context to a file, then docker context import CONTEXT FILE on another host. The destination host must have the Docker client installed.
interview.followUp: What other context operations are available? You can list, inspect, create, update, remove, show, and switch contexts with the docker context subcommands.

keyPoints: A context contains the settings needed to manage resources on one Docker daemon.
docker context ls marks the active context with an asterisk.
Created contexts are saved below the Docker configuration directory, with a separate metadata file for each context.
Use docker context use CONTEXT to select a different saved context.
DOCKER_CONTEXT selects a context through the environment and can override the saved selection.
Export a context to a file, then import that file on another host with the Docker client.
gotchas: docker context use changes the saved CLI default, so it affects other shells and later sessions that use the same Docker configuration.
DOCKER_CONTEXT takes priority over the saved context. Unset it when you want the configured default to apply.

docker cp.summary: Copies files and directories between a container and the local filesystem. It works with running or stopped containers and supports tar streams through standard input or output.
docker cp.explanation: The command transfers a file or directory between a container and the local computer. Container paths start at the container root, while local relative paths start in the directory where the command runs. Directory copies are recursive. The container may be running or stopped.
docker cp.syntax:
docker container cp [OPTIONS] CONTAINER:SRC_PATH DEST_PATH|-
docker cp [OPTIONS] SRC_PATH|- CONTAINER:DEST_PATH

parameters.name: SRC_PATH
parameters.description: The source file or directory. Use `CONTAINER:SRC_PATH` for a container source, or `-` for a tar archive from standard input.

parameters.name: DEST_PATH
parameters.description: The destination file or directory. Use `CONTAINER:DEST_PATH` for a container destination, or `-` for standard output.

parameters.name: CONTAINER
parameters.description: The name or ID of the container involved in the transfer.

docker cp.returns: Copies the selected file or directory, or streams a tar archive when `-` is used.

example.title: Copy a local file into a container
example.code: docker cp ./some_file CONTAINER:/work
example.explanation: Copies a local file into the container directory `/work`.

useCases.title: Send a local file to a container
useCases.scenario: Move a configuration file into a container for testing.

useCases.title: Copy files out of a container
useCases.scenario: Retrieve application logs from a container.

useCases.title: Stream a tar archive to standard output
useCases.scenario: Pipe a container file into another command.

useCases.title: Stream a tar archive from standard input
useCases.scenario: Load archived files into a container directory.

interview.question: What does `docker container cp` do?
interview.answer: It copies files or directories between a container and the local filesystem. The container can be running or stopped, and directory copies are recursive.
interview.followUp: What happens to ownership?

interview.question: What are the two main path forms?
interview.answer: Use `CONTAINER:SRC_PATH DEST_PATH` to copy out, or `SRC_PATH CONTAINER:DEST_PATH` to copy in. A container path is relative to the container root, so the first slash is optional.
interview.followUp: How can the command write a container file to standard output?

interview.question: What do the main options change?
interview.answer: Use `-a` to preserve source user and group ownership, and `-L` to follow symbolic links in the source path. Without `-a`, ownership is set to the destination user and primary group.
interview.followUp: What does `-` mean as the destination?

keyPoints: You can copy data whether the container is running or stopped.
Either side of the transfer can name one file or a directory.
Directory transfers include their contents and try to retain permissions.
A local relative path is resolved from the shell's current directory.
The `-L` option makes the source follow symbolic links.
gotchas: The destination's parent directory must already exist.
A standard-input source must be a tar archive, and the destination must be a directory.
Some system files and user-created mounts cannot be copied directly.

docker exec.summary: Runs a new executable inside a running container. It can use a terminal, environment variables, a different user, privileges, or a chosen working directory.
docker exec.explanation: Docker starts the given executable as a new process inside a running container. The process uses the container's default working directory unless `--workdir` changes it. It ends when the command ends and is not restarted with the container.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Options that control execution, input, terminal, environment, privileges, user, and working directory.

parameters.name: CONTAINER
parameters.description: The name or ID of a running container.

parameters.name: COMMAND [ARG...]
parameters.description: The executable to run, followed by its arguments.

docker exec.returns: The command's output and exit status, unless detached mode is used.

example.title: Run a command in a container
example.code:
docker run --name mycontainer -d -i -t alpine /bin/sh
docker exec -it mycontainer sh
docker exec -w /root mycontainer pwd
example.explanation: Starts an Alpine container, opens a shell in it, then runs `pwd` from `/root`.

useCases.title: Work inside a container
useCases.scenario: Open an interactive shell for inspection or administration.

useCases.title: Run a maintenance command
useCases.scenario: Run a one-time command without changing the container's main process.

useCases.title: Use detached mode
useCases.scenario: Start a long-running command in the background.

interview.question: What does `docker exec` do?
interview.answer: It runs a new command as a process inside a running container. The command runs only while the container's PID 1 process is running.
interview.followUp: What happens after the container restarts? The exec process is not restarted.

interview.question: How can you control the working directory?
interview.answer: The command is executed in the container's default working directory. Use `-w` or `--workdir` to choose another directory.
interview.followUp: What does `docker exec -w /root mycontainer pwd` print? It prints `/root`, assuming that directory exists.

interview.question: How do you set environment variables for an exec process?
interview.answer: Use `-e` or `--env` for variables available to the process started by that exec command. These variables do not become available to other processes in the container.
interview.followUp: Can `--env` change the environment of the main container process? No. It applies only to the new exec process.

keyPoints: Use `docker exec` to start an additional command without creating a new container.
Use `-d` or `--detach` when the command should run in the background.
Use `-i` or `--interactive` to keep standard input open.
Use `-t` or `--tty` to allocate a pseudo-terminal, often for an interactive shell.
Use `--privileged` when the exec process needs extended container privileges.
Use `-u` or `--user` to run the command as a selected user or user and group.
gotchas: The container's main process must still be running. The exec process is not restarted if the container restarts.
Pass an executable and its arguments. To use shell operators such as `&&`, explicitly run a shell with `sh -c`.
Unpause a paused container before using `docker exec`.

docker history.summary: Show the layer history of a Docker image. You can choose a platform and control the output format.
docker history.explanation: Docker reads the layers of the named image and prints information about how each layer was created. You can select a platform, change the output format, keep full values, or print only image IDs.

parameters.name: IMAGE
parameters.description: The image name, tag, or ID whose layer history should be shown.

parameters.name: --platform
parameters.description: Selects a platform variant, using `os[/arch[/variant]]`.

parameters.name: --format
parameters.description: Changes the output format.

parameters.name: -H, --human
parameters.description: Prints sizes and dates in human-readable form; default is true.

parameters.name: --no-trunc
parameters.description: Prevents output truncation.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Prints only image IDs.

docker history.returns: A formatted list of the image's layer history, or only image IDs when quiet mode is used.

example.title: Show selected history fields
example.code: docker image history --format '{{.ID}}: {{.CreatedSince}}' busybox
example.explanation: Prints each layer ID and its relative creation time, separated by a colon.

useCases.title: Inspect image layers
useCases.scenario: You want to understand which Dockerfile steps produced an image's layers.

useCases.title: Create custom output
useCases.scenario: You need machine-readable or selected fields for a script.

useCases.title: Inspect one platform
useCases.scenario: An image has multiple local platform variants.

interview.question: How do you display an image's layer history?
interview.answer: Use `docker image history IMAGE`. It lists image IDs, creation information, the command that created each layer, size, and comments.
interview.followUp: How can you avoid shortened values? Use `--no-trunc`, which prevents Docker from truncating the output.

interview.question: How can you customize the history output?
interview.answer: Use `--format` with a Go template. The `table` directive can include headers, while a template without `table` prints only the fields you declare.
interview.followUp: How would you print only image IDs? Add `-q` or `--quiet`.

interview.question: How do you inspect history for one platform variant?
interview.answer: Use `--platform` with a value such as `linux/amd64` or `linux/arm64/v8`. This selects the matching local platform variant.
interview.followUp: What happens if the variant is missing locally? Docker returns an error instead of showing history for another platform.

keyPoints: The command displays the recorded history of an image.
Human-readable sizes and dates are enabled by default with `--human`; disable that behavior by passing the option as false where supported.
Use `-q` or `--quiet` when the output should contain only image IDs.
Use `--no-trunc` to keep values from being shortened.
Use `--format` to produce table output, JSON output, or output defined by a Go template.
Platform values use operating system, optional architecture, and optional variant, such as `linux/amd64`.
gotchas: A requested platform must already exist in the local image cache. Otherwise, the command fails.
Without --platform, Docker uses the daemon's native platform when available; otherwise it uses the first available platform.

docker images.summary: `docker image ls` lists images stored locally. It can show hidden layers, digests, filtered results, custom templates, or only image IDs.
docker images.explanation: The command lists Docker images stored on the local system. By default, it shows top-level images, their repositories, tags, image IDs, creation time, and cumulative size. Use options to show hidden layers, digests, filtered results, or custom output.

parameters.name: [REPOSITORY[:TAG]]
parameters.description: Optional repository and optional tag to match exactly.

parameters.name: -a, --all
parameters.description: Show intermediate and dangling images.

parameters.name: --digests
parameters.description: Show image digests.

parameters.name: -f, --filter
parameters.description: Filter output with a key=value condition.

parameters.name: --format
parameters.description: Format output with a template or JSON.

parameters.name: --no-trunc
parameters.description: Do not shorten displayed values.

parameters.name: -q, --quiet
parameters.description: Show only image IDs.

parameters.name: --tree
parameters.description: Show multi-platform images as a tree; experimental and available with API 1.47+.

docker images.returns: A table of matching local images by default, or formatted image data when an output option is used.

example.title: List local images
example.code:
docker image ls

docker image ls --all --digests

docker image ls 'ubuntu:latest'
example.explanation: The first command lists normal images. The second also shows hidden layers and digests. The third lists only the exact repository and tag.

useCases.title: Review local images
useCases.scenario: Check which images are available before starting a container.

useCases.title: Find dangling images
useCases.scenario: Find untagged images before cleanup.

useCases.title: Filter images
useCases.scenario: Select images by repository, tag, label, age, or reference pattern.

useCases.title: Use machine-readable output
useCases.scenario: Pass image IDs to scripts or inspect image data as JSON.

interview.question: What does `docker image ls` do?
interview.answer: It lists images available locally. Normal output hides intermediate layers and dangling images, and shows repository, tag, image ID, creation time, and size.
interview.followUp: How would you show hidden layers and dangling images? Use `docker image ls --all`.

interview.question: How can you filter the image list?
interview.answer: Use `--filter` or `-f` with a `key=value` expression. Supported filters include `dangling`, `label`, `before`, `since`, and `reference`.
interview.followUp: How can you combine filters? Pass the option more than once, such as `--filter "dangling=true" --filter "reference=ubuntu:*"`.

interview.question: How can you customize the output?
interview.answer: Use `--format` with a Go template or the `json` directive. For example, `--format '{{.ID}}: {{.Repository}}'` prints selected fields without table headers.
interview.followUp: Which placeholders identify an image and its name? `.ID` gives the image ID, while `.Repository` and `.Tag` give its repository and tag.

keyPoints: The default listing shows top-level images with repository names, tags, and sizes.
Dangling images do not appear unless you use `--all` or a suitable filter.
Use `--all` to include intermediate layers and dangling images.
Use `--digests` to add content-addressable digest values to the listing.
Filters use the form `key=value`, and you can provide multiple filter options.
Use `--format` for Go-template output, table templates, or JSON lines.
gotchas: A repository or tag argument must match exactly. A shortened repository name returns no results.
One image can appear on several rows when it has multiple names or tags. Its size is counted only once.
The displayed size includes the image and its parent images. It is not only the newest layer.

docker init.summary: Creates Docker starter files for a project. It asks setup questions, then generates files such as a Dockerfile and Compose file so the project can run in a container.
docker init.explanation: Run `docker init` in a project directory. Docker Desktop asks questions about the application and creates starter files with suitable defaults. Review and adjust these files before starting the application with Docker Compose.

example.title: Create Docker starter files
example.code:
docker init

docker compose up --build
example.explanation: Run this in the project directory. Answer the prompts, review the generated files, then build and start the application.

useCases.title: Create a first Docker setup
useCases.scenario: A project has no container configuration yet.

useCases.title: Generate project templates
useCases.scenario: An application needs a starting Dockerfile and Compose file.

useCases.title: Start a containerized project
useCases.scenario: A team wants standard Docker-related files for a new application.

interview.question: What does `docker init` do?
interview.answer: `docker init` creates starter files for running a project in a container. It asks project-specific questions and generates `.dockerignore`, `Dockerfile`, `compose.yaml`, and `README.Docker.md`.
interview.followUp: What should you do after generation? Review the files and modify them for the application before running Compose.

interview.question: Where and how should you run `docker init`?
interview.answer: Run it from the project directory. The command walks through questions and uses the answers to create Docker-related files with defaults for the selected application type.
interview.followUp: Which application types are available? ASP.NET Core, Go, Java, Node, PHP with Apache, Python, Rust, and Other.

interview.question: How do you use the generated files?
interview.answer: After generation, start the application with `docker compose up --build`. The generated README contains more information, and the application is available on the port selected during setup.
interview.followUp: What must a PHP application owner check? Required PHP extensions may need to be added manually to the Dockerfile.

keyPoints: The command prepares the main files needed to run a project in a container.
This command is provided by Docker Desktop.
Run the command from the directory containing the project.
The command can create a `.dockerignore`, `Dockerfile`, `compose.yaml`, and `README.Docker.md`.
Templates cover common application types, including ASP.NET Core, Go, Java, Node, PHP with Apache, Python, and Rust.
Use Docker Compose with `--build` to build the image and start the generated application.
gotchas: If Docker finds existing generated files, it can overwrite them. Back up or rename those files first because the overwrite cannot be undone.
The generated files are templates, not guaranteed final project files. Choose a suitable template and tailor the results to the application.

docker inspect.summary: `docker inspect` returns detailed information about Docker objects. It normally prints a JSON array, and it can use Go templates to select or format fields.
docker inspect.explanation: Docker inspect returns detailed information about a Docker object. It normally prints a JSON array, or it can run a Go template once for each object.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Options such as `--format`, `--size`, and `--type`.

parameters.name: NAME|ID [NAME|ID...]
parameters.description: One or more Docker object names or IDs.

docker inspect.returns: Detailed information about the specified Docker objects, normally as a JSON array.

example.title: Print a container image name
example.code: docker inspect --type=container --format='{{.Config.Image}}' my-container
example.explanation: This prints the image name configured for the container.

useCases.title: Read a field with a Go template
useCases.scenario: You need a selected value instead of the full inspection result.

useCases.title: Disambiguate an object name
useCases.scenario: A name may refer to different object types.

useCases.title: Check container sizes
useCases.scenario: You need container storage information.

interview.question: What does `docker inspect` do?
interview.answer: It displays detailed, low-level information about Docker objects. Without a format option, the result is a JSON array.
interview.followUp: How can output be changed? Use `--format` with `json` or a Go template, which runs for each result.

interview.question: Why use the `--type` option?
interview.answer: Use `--type`, such as `--type=volume`, when an object name could match more than one object kind. This removes the ambiguity.
interview.followUp: Which object types can be selected? The documented choices include config, container, image, node, network, secret, service, volume, task, and plugin.

interview.question: What does `docker inspect --size` add?
interview.answer: Use `--size` or `-s` for a container. It adds `SizeRootFs`, the total file size, and `SizeRw`, the size changed relative to the image.
interview.followUp: Does the container need to be running? No. The option also works for stopped containers.

keyPoints: Use this command to view detailed information about Docker-managed objects.
The default output is a JSON array.
Use `--format` or `-f` to print JSON or evaluate a Go template.
Use `--size` or `-s` to include container file-size data.
Use `--type` to limit inspection to one Docker object type.
For numeric field names in template maps, use the template `index` function.
gotchas: An object name or ID can be ambiguous when different object types share it. Use `--type` to select the expected type.
The `--size` option applies only to containers, including stopped containers.
Size inspection also works when the container is stopped.

docker load.summary: Load an image or repository from a tar archive or standard input. Docker restores the images and their tags, and it can read several compressed archive formats.
docker load.explanation: Docker reads an image or repository from a tar archive or standard input. It restores the image data and its tags; compressed archives using gzip, bzip2, xz, or zstd are also supported.

parameters.name: --input, -i
parameters.description: Read the tar archive from this file instead of standard input.

parameters.name: --platform
parameters.description: Load only the selected platform variants. Use comma-separated `os[/arch[/variant]]` values.

parameters.name: --quiet, -q
parameters.description: Hide loading output.

docker load.returns: The loaded images and tags are added to the local Docker image store. Normal output reports loaded images unless quiet mode is used.

example.title: Load an image archive
example.code:
docker image load --input app.tar

docker image ls app
example.explanation: Reads the tar archive and adds its images and tags to the local Docker image store.

useCases.title: Import an image archive
useCases.scenario: You received an exported Docker image archive and need it locally.

useCases.title: Transfer images offline
useCases.scenario: You need to move images between machines without pulling from a registry.

useCases.title: Select a platform
useCases.scenario: An archive contains several architectures, but the host needs one.

interview.question: What does `docker image load` do?
interview.answer: `docker image load` imports an image or repository from a tar archive or standard input. It restores both the images and their tags.
interview.followUp: How can you load only one platform variant? Use `--platform`, such as `linux/amd64`; the option accepts a comma-separated platform list.

interview.question: How do you load an image from a file?
interview.answer: Use `--input` followed by the archive path, for example `docker image load --input app.tar`. The command reads the archive instead of standard input.
interview.followUp: Can the archive be compressed? Yes. The command supports gzip, bzip2, xz, and zstd compressed archives.

interview.question: How do you choose a platform during loading?
interview.answer: `--platform` selects the platform variants to load. Its value uses `os[/arch[/variant]]`, and multiple values are separated by commas.
interview.followUp: What happens when the option is omitted? Docker loads all platform variants contained in the archive.

keyPoints: The command imports an image or repository stored in a tar archive.
Input can come from a file or standard input, and restored tags remain available.
The archive may use gzip, bzip2, xz, or zstd compression.
`--platform` limits loading to the platform or platforms you specify.
Platform values use an operating system, architecture, and optional variant, separated by slashes.
Use `--quiet` to hide the normal loading output.
gotchas: Without `--platform`, Docker loads every platform variant in the archive. Use a platform value to load only selected variants.
Use `--input` when the archive is a file. Without it, provide the archive through standard input.

docker login.summary: Authenticate Docker to a public or private registry. Use browser-based device login for Docker Hub, or provide a username and token or password for another registry.
docker login.explanation: Docker checks your credentials for a public or private registry. It saves them in the configured credential store, such as the operating system keychain; without one, it uses base64-encoded data in the Docker configuration file.

parameters.name: --password, -p
parameters.description: Password or personal access token; use `-` with `-p` to read it from standard input.

parameters.name: --password-stdin
parameters.description: Read the password or personal access token from standard input.

parameters.name: --username, -u
parameters.description: Registry username.

parameters.name: SERVER
parameters.description: Registry hostname, with an optional port.

docker login.returns: The page documents successful authentication as `Login Succeeded`; it does not define a separate return value.

example.title: Sign in with a token from standard input
example.code: printf '%s' "$DOCKER_PAT" | docker login --username myuser --password-stdin registry.example.com
example.explanation: This signs in to the registry without putting the token in shell history or log files.

useCases.title: Docker Hub device login
useCases.scenario: Sign in to Docker Hub interactively from a local terminal.

useCases.title: Non-interactive registry login
useCases.scenario: Authenticate a script or CI job without exposing a token in command arguments.

useCases.title: Private registry access
useCases.scenario: Access a private self-hosted registry before pulling or pushing images.

interview.question: What does `docker login` do?
interview.answer: `docker login` authenticates Docker with a public or private registry. With Docker Hub, it uses a browser-based device flow by default; specifying `--username` selects command-line credential entry.
interview.followUp: How should a CI job authenticate? Use a personal access token and pass it through `--password-stdin`, so the secret is not placed in shell history or log files.

interview.question: How do you log in to a self-hosted registry?
interview.answer: Use `docker login registry.example.com` for a registry on the default ports. Include a port when the registry uses another port, such as `registry.example.com:1337`.
interview.followUp: What registry name should not be used? A name with a URL path, such as `registry.example.com/foo/`, can fail; use the host and optional port only.

interview.question: Where does Docker store registry credentials?
interview.answer: Docker saves login credentials in the configured credential store. Docker Desktop uses the operating system keychain, while a non-Desktop setup can configure `credsStore` in the Docker configuration file.
interview.followUp: What happens without a credential store? Docker writes base64-encoded credentials to `config.json`, which is less secure than using a credential store.

keyPoints: Use the command for registries that require authentication before pulling or pushing images.
A plain `docker login` opens a Docker Hub device-code sign-in flow instead of asking for a password.
Add the registry port when it does not use port 443 or 80.
Use `--password-stdin` to provide a password or personal access token from standard input.
Set `credsStore` to the credential helper suffix, such as `osxkeychain`, not the full executable name.
gotchas: Use only the registry host and optional port. Do not add a path such as `/foo/`. Docker Hub is the documented historical exception for `/v1/`.
For scripts and CI, use `--password-stdin` instead of putting the password directly in the command.
Configure a credential store when possible. Base64 encoding does not provide the same protection.

docker logs.summary: Fetch and display a container's logs. You can follow new output, limit lines or time, and add timestamps or extra details.

Options can limit the time range, select the number of lines, add timestamps or details, or keep the output open for new lines.

interview.question: What does `docker container logs` display?
interview.answer: It retrieves the logs available when the command runs. With `--follow`, it also continues streaming new output from the container's standard output and standard error.
interview.followUp: What if the application writes to a file? The command may not display that file because it reads the container's standard output and standard error, not arbitrary application log files.

interview.question: How do you limit the amount of log output?
interview.answer: Use `--tail` to choose how many lines to show from the end. The default is `all`, so Docker returns all available lines unless a limit is set.
interview.followUp: How would you inspect only recent output while watching for new lines? Use `--tail` together with `--follow`, such as `docker logs --tail 50 --follow CONTAINER`.

interview.question: How do time filters and timestamps work?
interview.answer: Use `--since` to show logs after a timestamp or relative duration, and `--until` to stop before a timestamp or relative duration. `--since` can be combined with `--follow` or `--tail`.
interview.followUp: How can you make entries easier to compare by time? Add `--timestamps`; Docker uses RFC3339Nano timestamps and pads the nanosecond part when needed.

keyPoints: Run `docker container logs CONTAINER` to retrieve the container's stored log output.
Without `--follow`, the command returns the records available when it starts instead of continuously waiting for more.
Add `--follow` or `-f` to keep receiving new output as the container writes it.
Use `--timestamps` or `-t` to add precise timestamps to each log entry.
Combine `--since` with `--follow` or `--tail` to inspect a time range while limiting or continuing the output.
gotchas: An application might write to its own log files instead of standard output and standard error, so this command might not show those messages.
Use a non-negative integer with `--tail`; invalid values cause Docker to use all available lines.

interview.question: When should you use bridge versus overlay?
interview.answer: Use a bridge network for containers on one Docker Engine. Use an overlay network when containers need to communicate across multiple Docker hosts in Swarm mode.
interview.followUp: How can a manually started container join a Swarm overlay network? Create it with --attachable. Without that option, the default restriction blocks manual container attachment.

interview.question: How do you attach containers to a network?
interview.answer: Start a container with --network, or use docker network connect after the container is running. Containers on the same network can communicate by container name or IP address.
interview.followUp: What does --internal change? It prevents normal communication with other networks by omitting a default route and adding firewall rules, while containers on that network can still communicate with each other.

interview.question: How can you control a network's IP range?
interview.answer: Docker creates a non-overlapping subnet by default. You can set --subnet, --gateway, --ip-range, and --aux-address when you need specific addressing.
interview.followUp: Can an overlay network have multiple subnets? Yes, overlay networks and compatible plugins can support multiple subnetworks; a bridge network supports only one.

keyPoints: The command group manages network creation, inspection, listing, removal, pruning, connection, and disconnection.
If you omit --driver, Docker creates a bridge network.
Bridge networks isolate containers on one Docker Engine.
An overlay network is the choice for communication across multiple Docker hosts.
Containers on the same network can reach each other by name or IP address.
Docker chooses a non-overlapping subnet unless you provide network addressing options.
gotchas: A bridge network supports only one subnet when you create it.
A Swarm-scoped overlay network does not accept manually started containers unless you add --attachable.
An ingress network cannot be removed while services still depend on it.

interview.question: What does docker compose ps do?
interview.answer: It lists containers for a Compose project, including their current status and exposed ports. By default, it displays only running containers.
interview.followUp: How would you include stopped containers? Add the --all option, which also includes containers created by the run command.

interview.question: How do you list stopped containers or limit the result?

interview.question: How can command output be used by another tool?

The documented filter is status; it is not a general filter for every container property.

parameters.name: --quiet, -q
parameters.description: Suppress verbose output.

docker pull.returns: The downloaded image is stored locally; the command reports its digest and pull status.

example.explanation: Downloads the Ubuntu 24.04 image from Docker Hub.

interview.question: What does `docker image pull` do?
interview.answer: It downloads an image from a registry. The usual form is `docker image pull NAME[:TAG|@DIGEST]`; `docker pull` is an alias.
interview.followUp: How do you make the image selection immutable? Pull it with a digest, such as `ubuntu@sha256:...`, instead of a tag.

interview.question: What is the difference between a tag and a digest here?
interview.answer: If the command has no tag, Docker uses `latest`. A tag identifies a changeable image version, while a digest identifies the exact image.
interview.followUp: What happens when a pinned image receives a security update? Docker does not fetch it until the digest is changed.

interview.question: How can you control what gets pulled?
interview.answer: Use `--all-tags` to download every tagged image in a repository. Use `--platform` to choose a platform when the server supports multi-platform images.
interview.followUp: How can you reduce command output? Add `--quiet`; this suppresses verbose output.

keyPoints: The command downloads an image from a registry into the local Docker environment.
The shorter `docker pull` command is an alias for `docker image pull`.
If no tag appears in the image name, Docker selects the `latest` tag.
Use an image digest instead of a tag when you need an exact image version.
Add `--all-tags` to download all tagged images in a repository.
The `--platform` option selects the target platform when the registry supports multi-platform images.
gotchas: Leaving out the tag selects `latest`, which might change when you pull again.
A digest keeps the selected image version fixed, so updated security fixes are not pulled automatically.
Slow connections can have timeout problems because three layers download concurrently; the daemon setting can lower this.

docker tag my-app my-namespace/my-repo:v1.0
docker push my-namespace/my-repo:v1.0
example.explanation: Log in, give the image a repository tag, then upload that tagged image.

useCases.title: Deploy from a registry

interview.question: How do you push a local image to a repository?
interview.answer: Use `docker tag` to give the local image a name that includes the namespace and repository. Then run `docker push` with that complete tag.
interview.followUp: What must happen before the push? The client must authenticate with the registry, usually with `docker login`.

interview.question: Why should an image be tagged before pushing?
interview.answer: A tag identifies where the image should be published and which tag name it should use. For example, `my-namespace/my-repo:v1.0` names the namespace, repository, and version tag.
interview.followUp: What can happen if the namespace is wrong? The registry can deny access because the account may not own or have permission to that repository.

interview.question: What does `docker push` upload?
interview.answer: Run `docker push` followed by the full image tag, such as `docker push my-namespace/my-repo:v1.0`. Docker then uploads the image layers to the registry.
interview.followUp: How can you check that the push worked on Docker Hub? Open the repository and inspect its Tags list for the pushed tag.

A repository tag can include a version, such as `v1.0`, after the repository name.
Run `docker push` with the complete image tag to upload the image.

After pushing, check the repository's Tags area to confirm that the new tag is present.
gotchas: Log in before pushing. Without authentication, the registry may reject the upload.
An access-denied error can mean that you are not logged in or that the image tag uses the wrong Docker username.

docker rm.explanation: The command removes one or more image references from the local host. interview.question: What happens when an image has multiple tags?
interview.answer: `docker image rm` removes local image references. If several tags point to one image, removing one tag only removes that tag; removing the final tag removes the image.
interview.followUp: How can you remove every tag that points to an image ID? Use `docker image rm --force IMAGE_ID`, which forces removal of all matching tags and the image.

interview.followUp: What happens without `--force`? Docker warns that the content is shared and cancels the removal.

Without a platform filter, Docker removes all platform variants present for the selected image.

An image used by a running container needs `--force` before Docker can remove it.

interview.question: What is the basic form of `docker run`?
interview.answer: The command is `docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE[:TAG|@DIGEST] [COMMAND] [ARG...]`. Docker creates and starts a new container from the image, pulling the image if needed.

interview.question: How do foreground and detached containers differ?
interview.answer: By default, the container runs in the foreground. The `-d` or `--detach` option starts it in the background, and commands such as `docker logs` and `docker attach` can then be used to interact with it.
interview.followUp: How can you keep standard input open for a shell? Combine `-i` with `-t`, for example `docker run -it ubuntu:24.04 /bin/bash`.

interview.question: When should you use a volume or bind mount?
interview.answer: A volume stores persistent container data and can be shared between containers. A bind mount maps a host path into the container; it is read-write by default and changes are reflected on the host.
interview.followUp: Which mount syntax does Docker recommend? Use `--mount`; Docker supports `--volume`, but the documentation recommends `--mount`.

docker scout cves.returns: Prints vulnerabilities to standard output by default, or writes a report to the file named by --output.

example.title: Check critical vulnerabilities
example.code: docker scout cves --only-severity critical my-image:latest
example.explanation: This checks the image and shows only critical vulnerabilities.

useCases.title: Find image vulnerabilities
useCases.scenario: You need to inspect an image before deployment.

useCases.title: Export SARIF
useCases.scenario: A build pipeline needs a structured security report.

useCases.title: Filter with EPSS
useCases.scenario: You want to focus on likely exploitable issues.

useCases.title: Analyze non-image inputs
useCases.scenario: Your input is an archive, OCI directory, or SBOM.

interview.question: What does docker scout cves do?
interview.answer: The command analyzes a software artifact for vulnerabilities. It supports images, OCI layout directories, saved-image tarballs, and local files or directories.
interview.followUp: How can you analyze an SPDX file? Use the sbom:// prefix, or pipe the SPDX output to docker scout cves sbom://.

interview.question: How do you export the vulnerability report?
interview.answer: Use --format to choose the report format and --output to write the report to a file. For example, --format sarif --output report.json creates a SARIF JSON report.
interview.followUp: Why might SARIF be useful? It gives security tools a structured report that they can consume.

interview.question: How is vulnerability severity determined?
interview.answer: Docker Scout uses advisory data to assign vulnerability severity. When available from the selected advisory source, it prefers CVSS v4 data over CVSS v3 data.
interview.followUp: What happens when no CVSS score exists? The vulnerability is categorized as Unspecified.

keyPoints: Use docker scout cves to find vulnerabilities in an image or supported artifact.
The command supports images, OCI directories, docker save tarballs, and local files or directories.
A normal invocation can use an image name such as alpine or a registry image reference.
EPSS data changes daily, and the latest available score is shown by default.
gotchas: Without an image argument, Docker Scout checks the most recently built image.
Use the matching source prefix when the input is not a normal image reference.
A vulnerability may be marked Unspecified when no source provides a CVSS score.

docker start.summary: Starts one or more existing stopped containers. You can optionally attach input, output, error streams, and signal forwarding.
docker start.explanation: Docker starts an existing container that is not running. You identify the container by name or ID. The container keeps the settings it received when it was created. You can attach to its output and input when starting it.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Command options such as --attach, --interactive, --detach-keys, and checkpoint options.

parameters.name: CONTAINER [CONTAINER...]
parameters.description: Name or ID of the container to start. More containers can be supplied.

docker start.returns: The page does not specify a return value.

example.title: Create and start a container
example.code:
docker create --name my_container nginx
docker start my_container
example.explanation: Creates a stopped container from the nginx image, then starts it.

useCases.title: Resume a container
useCases.scenario: Start a container that was previously created or stopped.

useCases.title: Start multiple containers
useCases.scenario: Start several stopped containers in one command.

useCases.title: Attach to container streams
useCases.scenario: Connect a terminal to a container while starting it.

interview.question: What does docker container start do?
interview.answer: The command starts one or more existing stopped containers. Its syntax is docker container start followed by options and one or more container names or IDs.
interview.followUp: How would you create a container without starting it? Use docker container create, then run docker container start later.

interview.question: What are the attachment options?
interview.answer: The --attach option connects the container's standard output and error streams and forwards signals. The --interactive option attaches the container's standard input.
interview.followUp: What option changes the detach key sequence? Use --detach-keys with the desired key sequence.

interview.question: Is docker start a different command?
interview.answer: docker start is an alias for docker container start. Both commands start stopped containers and accept the same documented options.
interview.followUp: How can you start several containers? Put multiple container names or IDs after the options.

keyPoints: The command starts one or more containers whose current state is stopped.
The command accepts options, then one required container and additional optional containers.
docker start is the short alias for docker container start.
The --interactive or -i option connects the container's standard input.
The --detach-keys option changes the keys used to detach from an attached container.
gotchas: This command starts containers that already exist and are stopped. It does not create a new container.
Use --attach when you need the container's output or signal forwarding connected to your terminal.

docker stats.summary: `docker container stats` streams resource usage for running containers. It can show CPU, memory, network I/O, block I/O, and process or thread counts, with options for all containers and custom output.
docker stats.explanation: Docker continuously displays runtime resource data for running containers. You can name specific containers, include stopped containers with --all, or change the output with Go-template formatting. Stopped containers do not provide statistics.

parameters.name: -a, --all
parameters.description: Show all containers, including stopped containers.

parameters.name: --format
parameters.description: Format output with a table, JSON, or Go template.

parameters.name: CONTAINER...
parameters.description: One or more container names or IDs to monitor.

docker stats.returns: A live stream of container resource statistics. Stopped containers return no data.

example.title: Show one formatted snapshot
example.code: docker stats --no-stream --format 'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}' nginx
example.explanation: Shows one snapshot for the nginx container with its name, CPU percentage, and memory usage.

useCases.title: Monitor live usage
useCases.scenario: Watch running containers during development or troubleshooting.

useCases.title: Take one snapshot
useCases.scenario: Check a single container once in a script.

useCases.title: Format statistics
useCases.scenario: Create compact or machine-readable output.

useCases.title: Check resource limits
useCases.scenario: Compare usage with a configured memory limit.

interview.question: What does docker stats do?
interview.answer: docker stats displays a live stream for running containers. Give it container names or IDs to limit the stream, or use --all to show all containers.
interview.followUp: How can you collect one machine-readable sample? Use --no-stream with --format and a JSON Go-template, such as {{ json . }}.

interview.question: What information does the default output show?
interview.answer: The default output includes CPU percentage, memory usage and limit, memory percentage, network I/O, block I/O, and PIDs on Linux. Windows output differs and does not provide MemPerc or PIDs.
interview.followUp: Which fields are unavailable on Windows? MemPerc and PIDs are not available there.

interview.question: How can stats output be customized?
interview.answer: The --format option accepts Go templates. Placeholders include .Name, .ID, .CPUPerc, .MemUsage, .NetIO, .BlockIO, .MemPerc, and .PIDs; the table directive adds headers.
interview.followUp: How would you omit headers? Use a template without the table directive, for example {{.Container}}: {{.CPUPerc}}.

keyPoints: The command keeps updating resource statistics for running containers.
Use --all to include stopped containers; without it, Docker shows only running containers.
Use --format to select table, JSON, or a custom Go-template output.
Memory output shows current use together with the container's allowed limit.
NET I/O reports network data received and sent by the container.
PIDs reports the processes and threads created by the container.
gotchas: Naming a stopped container does not produce statistics. Use --all to include stopped containers in the output, but their values are empty or zero.
On Linux, the CLI subtracts cache from memory usage, while the statistics API returns total usage and cache separately.
PIDS counts processes and kernel threads, not only ordinary processes. A high value can point to excessive thread creation.

docker stop.summary: Stops one or more running containers. Docker sends a stop signal, waits for a grace period, and then force-kills containers that do not exit.
docker stop.explanation: Docker sends a stop signal to the container's main process. It waits for the configured timeout. If the process is still running, Docker ends it with SIGKILL. The signal can come from the command option, the image, or the container configuration.

parameters.name: --signal, -s
parameters.description: Signal to send to the container. It may be a signal name such as SIGKILL or an unsigned number such as 9.

parameters.name: --timeout, -t
parameters.description: Seconds to wait after sending the stop signal before killing the container. Use -1 to wait indefinitely.

parameters.name: CONTAINER
parameters.description: Name or ID of one or more running containers.

docker stop.returns: The command stops the selected container or containers. The page does not specify a return value.

example.title: Stop a container
example.code: docker stop my_container
example.explanation: Sends the container's configured stop signal, then waits before forcefully killing it if needed.

useCases.title: Stop one container
useCases.scenario: A container is running normally and should be shut down.

useCases.title: Stop multiple containers
useCases.scenario: Several containers need to stop together.

useCases.title: Set a custom wait time
useCases.scenario: An application needs a longer time to finish cleanup.

useCases.title: Send a different signal
useCases.scenario: A process ignores the normal stop signal.

interview.question: What does `docker container stop` do?
interview.answer: `docker container stop` stops one or more running containers. It sends the selected stop signal, waits for the timeout, and then uses SIGKILL if the container has not exited.
interview.followUp: How can the stop signal be changed? Use `--signal` for the stop command, or configure it with the image's `STOPSIGNAL` instruction or the `--stop-signal` option when creating the container.

interview.question: How do you choose the signal used to stop a container?
interview.answer: The `--signal` option selects the signal sent to the container. It accepts a name such as `SIGKILL` or an unsigned number such as `9`.
interview.followUp: What happens if no signal is configured? Docker uses `SIGTERM` by default.

interview.question: What does the stop timeout control?
interview.answer: The `--timeout` option sets how many seconds Docker waits after sending the stop signal. If the container is still running when the wait ends, Docker forcibly kills it with `SIGKILL`.
interview.followUp: How can Docker wait forever? Set `--timeout` to `-1`; the daemon then waits indefinitely.

keyPoints: The command can stop one container or several containers in one invocation.
By default, the container's main process receives SIGTERM first.
An image can define a different initial signal with Dockerfile `STOPSIGNAL`.
Container creation can set the initial stop signal with `--stop-signal`.
Use `--signal` when the stop command must send a chosen signal.
The `--timeout` value specifies the wait in seconds before forced termination.
gotchas: Using `--timeout -1` makes Docker wait without a time limit for the container to exit.
A shortened container ID works when it uniquely identifies one container.

Docker Swarm.summary: Docker Swarm mode manages a cluster of Docker Engine hosts. Managers maintain the desired state of services, and workers run the resulting container tasks.
Docker Swarm.explanation: A swarm is a group of Docker Engine hosts in Swarm mode. Managers control membership and desired state, while workers run assigned tasks. A service describes containers, commands, replicas, networks, storage, and ports. Managers continually compare the actual cluster with the desired state and replace failed tasks.

example.title: Create and scale a service
example.code:
docker swarm init
docker service create --name web --publish published=8080,target=80 nginx
docker service scale web=3
docker service ls
example.explanation: This creates a swarm, starts a replicated web service, changes it to three tasks, and lists the service.

useCases.title: Replicated application services
useCases.scenario: Run an application across several Docker Engine hosts with a declared number of replicas.

useCases.title: Node-wide services
useCases.scenario: Keep one copy of a service on every available node.

useCases.title: Desired-state recovery
useCases.scenario: Replace containers after a worker or task fails.

useCases.title: Multi-host service networking
useCases.scenario: Expose services across multiple hosts using Docker overlay networking.

interview.question: What is a Docker swarm?
interview.answer: A swarm is a group of Docker Engine hosts running in Swarm mode. Managers handle membership, orchestration, and desired-state maintenance; workers execute tasks assigned by managers.
interview.followUp: Can a host have both roles? Yes. A Docker host can be a manager, a worker, or both.

interview.question: What is the difference between a service and a task?
interview.answer: A service is the desired definition of work, including the image, command, replica count, networks, storage, and published ports. A task is a running container that belongs to a service and is managed by a swarm manager.
interview.followUp: How does a global service differ from a replicated service? A global service runs one task on every available node, while a replicated service runs the configured number of tasks across nodes.

interview.question: How does Swarm mode maintain availability?
interview.answer: The manager continuously compares the actual cluster with the desired state. If a node fails and its tasks stop, the manager schedules replacement tasks on available nodes.
interview.followUp: What happens when a service is scaled? The manager adds or removes tasks until the configured replica count is reached.

keyPoints: Swarm mode is part of Docker Engine and manages a cluster of Docker Engines.
Each host can act as a manager, a worker, or both.
A service records the desired replica count and resource, network, storage, and port settings.
Replicated services spread the configured number of tasks across swarm nodes.
When tasks fail, the manager places replacement replicas on available workers.
gotchas: Use a manager to create or change swarm services. A standalone container is not managed by the swarm.
Managers also run service tasks unless configured as manager-only nodes.
Global services do not use a fixed replica count. They place one task on each available node.
Swarm mode is built into Docker Engine. It is different from the older Docker Classic Swarm project.

docker system prune.summary: Remove unused Docker containers, networks, images, and build cache. Use --all for unused tagged images and --volumes for unused anonymous volumes.
docker system prune.explanation: Docker removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and unused build cache. Add --all to include unused images, or --volumes to include unused anonymous volumes. Use --filter to narrow what is removed and --force to skip the confirmation prompt.

parameters.name: -a, --all
parameters.description: Remove unused images, including images that are not dangling.

parameters.name: --filter
parameters.description: Limit cleanup with filter expressions, such as label=<key>=<value>.

parameters.name: -f, --force
parameters.description: Skip the confirmation prompt.

parameters.name: --volumes
parameters.description: Also remove unused anonymous volumes.

docker system prune.returns: The command reports deleted containers, networks, and images, plus the total reclaimed space.

example.title: Prune older unused objects
example.code: docker system prune --filter "until=24h" --force
example.explanation: Removes matching unused Docker objects without asking for confirmation.

useCases.title: Clean several unused object types
useCases.scenario: A development host has stopped containers, old networks, dangling images, and build cache using disk space.

useCases.title: Run cleanup without a prompt
useCases.scenario: A script or CI job must clean Docker data without waiting for input.

useCases.title: Limit cleanup with filters
useCases.scenario: You want to remove only objects that match a condition, such as age or a label.

interview.question: What does docker system prune remove by default?
interview.answer: It removes stopped containers, networks unused by containers, dangling images, and unused build cache. It does not remove volumes unless --volumes is supplied.
interview.followUp: How would you remove unused tagged images too? Add --all, which removes unused images instead of limiting image cleanup to dangling images.

interview.question: How does volume pruning work?
interview.answer: Use --volumes to include unused anonymous volumes. Docker leaves volumes out by default to reduce the risk of deleting data that no current container uses.
interview.followUp: How do you target unused named volumes? Use docker volume prune --all, because system prune --volumes is for anonymous volumes.

interview.question: How can you make pruning non-interactive and narrower?
interview.answer: The command asks for confirmation by default. Use --force or -f to run without that prompt, and use --filter to limit the objects considered, such as with until=24h.
interview.followUp: What does a time filter change? It limits pruning to objects matching the filter, so it can reduce the cleanup scope.

keyPoints: The command cleans unused containers, networks, images, and build cache in one operation.
The --all option also removes unused tagged images.
The --filter option accepts filter expressions, including label-based filters.
The --force option makes the command run without asking for confirmation.
gotchas: Volumes are not removed unless you add --volumes. Even then, this command targets unused anonymous volumes; unused named volumes need docker volume prune --all.
This command can remove build cache, including BuildKit cache mounts. Use docker builder prune when you want to clean only build cache.

docker tag.summary: Creates a new tag that refers to an existing Docker image. The source and target can use image names, IDs, registries, namespaces, repositories, and tags.
docker tag.explanation: Docker image tag creates another name for an existing local image. The source can be an image ID or an image name, and the target can include a registry, namespace, repository, and tag. It does not build or upload the image.

parameters.name: SOURCE_IMAGE[:TAG]
parameters.description: Existing image ID or local image reference. Its tag is optional.

parameters.name: TARGET_IMAGE[:TAG]
parameters.description: New image reference. It may include a registry host, port, namespace, repository, and optional tag.

docker tag.returns: Creates a tag reference for the source image. The documentation does not specify a command output or return value.

example.title: Create a local image tag
example.code:
docker tag httpd fedora/httpd:version1.0
docker image ls fedora/httpd:version1.0
example.explanation: This gives the local `httpd` image a second name and tag. The second command lists the new reference.

useCases.title: Name an image for publishing
useCases.scenario: Prepare a local image with the name and version required by a registry.

useCases.title: Create an additional local reference
useCases.scenario: Give one local image a second name for a different deployment or release label.

useCases.title: Tag by image ID
useCases.scenario: Use an image ID when the image does not have a convenient local name.

interview.question: What does `docker image tag` do?
interview.answer: It creates a tag that refers to an existing image. The source may be an image ID or a local image name, and the target becomes another image reference.
interview.followUp: Does tagging copy the image layers? No. It creates another reference to the same local image.

interview.question: What is the command syntax?
interview.answer: The syntax is `docker image tag SOURCE_IMAGE[:TAG] TARGET_IMAGE[:TAG]`. Both source and target may include optional tags.
interview.followUp: What happens when the target has no tag? Docker uses `latest` as the default tag.

interview.question: How is an image reference structured?
interview.answer: An image reference may contain a host, port, namespace, repository, and tag. If the host is absent, Docker uses Docker Hub; if the namespace is absent, it uses `library`.
interview.followUp: How would you prepare an image for Docker Hub? Add the namespace and repository in the target, then run `docker push` with that same reference.

keyPoints: The command gives an existing image a new target reference.
The source and target image references may each include an optional tag.
An image ID can be used as the source.
A local image name can also be used as the source.
The host identifies the registry location in an image reference.
The namespace commonly identifies a user or organization, while the repository identifies the image.
A tagged reference can be uploaded with `docker push`.
gotchas: If the source omits its tag, Docker uses the local `latest` tag.
If the target omits its tag, Docker assigns `latest`.
Tagging only creates the reference locally. Use `docker push` to upload it.

docker top.summary: docker is the base command for the Docker CLI. Use it with a subcommand to manage Docker resources and use --help to view command help.
docker top.explanation: The Docker CLI is the main command-line client for Docker. Type docker followed by a command and its options. Add --help after a command to display that command's usage and available options.

parameters.name: command and arguments
parameters.description: Docker CLI subcommand and its arguments, options, image, or command data.

example.title: Run a container
example.code: docker run --name web nginx
example.explanation: Creates and starts a container named web from the nginx image.

useCases.title: Run a container
useCases.scenario: You need to create and start a container from an image.

useCases.title: View command help
useCases.scenario: You need to learn a command's available options.

useCases.title: Run with required privileges
useCases.scenario: Your Docker setup requires permission to access the Docker daemon.

interview.question: What is docker?
interview.answer: docker is the base command for the Docker CLI. You add a Docker command, options, and its arguments after it.
interview.followUp: How can you discover the options for a command? Run that command with --help, such as docker run --help.

interview.question: How do you view help for a Docker command?
interview.answer: Run the command followed by --help. For example, docker run --help shows the command usage and its options.
interview.followUp: Does --help only work with docker run? No. The documentation says it can be used to list help for any command.

interview.question: Why might a Docker command need sudo?
interview.answer: The Docker CLI may need sudo, depending on the Docker system configuration. Without sudo, an administrator can create a Unix group named docker and add users to it.
interview.followUp: Who should make this configuration? A system administrator should create the group and add the required users.

keyPoints: Use docker as the starting command for Docker CLI operations.
Add --help after a Docker command to see its usage and options.
The docker run command accepts options, an image, and optional command arguments.
docker run creates and starts a new container from an image.
gotchas: Your system setup may require sudo before each Docker command.
A system administrator can configure a docker Unix group so users do not need sudo.

docker volume.summary: Manage Docker volumes with subcommands that create, inspect, list, remove, or prune them. Volumes persist independently from containers and can be mounted into one or more containers.
docker volume.explanation: Docker volumes are data stores that Docker creates and manages outside a container. A container can mount a volume at a path, and Docker can create the volume automatically when the container starts. The volume remains after the container is removed until you remove it separately.

parameters.name: COMMAND
parameters.description: The Docker volume subcommand, such as create, inspect, ls, prune, rm, or update.

docker volume.returns: The selected volume subcommand performs its requested volume operation and writes command output to the terminal.

example.title: Create and use a volume
example.code:
docker volume create my-vol
docker volume ls
docker run -d --name devtest --mount source=my-vol,target=/data nginx:latest
docker inspect devtest
docker container stop devtest
docker container rm devtest
docker volume rm my-vol
example.explanation: This creates a volume, mounts it in a container, checks the mount, and then removes the container and volume.

useCases.title: Persist container data
useCases.scenario: Keep database or application files after replacing a container.

useCases.title: Share data between containers
useCases.scenario: Let multiple containers read or write shared files.

useCases.title: Connect external storage
useCases.scenario: Use storage such as NFS, CIFS, or another external system.

useCases.title: Avoid host path dependence
useCases.scenario: Keep Docker-managed storage separate from host directory paths.

interview.question: What does docker volume do?
interview.answer: docker volume manages Docker volumes. Its subcommands can create, inspect, list, remove, or prune volumes.
interview.followUp: How can you identify a volume's host location? Use docker volume inspect and check the Mountpoint field.

interview.question: Why use a Docker volume?
interview.answer: A volume is managed by Docker and can persist data beyond a container's lifetime. Docker can create it explicitly or when a container starts with a new volume name.
interview.followUp: Why choose a volume over a bind mount? Volumes are managed by Docker, easier to back up or migrate, and work with Linux and Windows containers.

interview.question: How do you mount a volume?
interview.answer: Use --mount source=NAME,target=PATH or -v NAME:PATH. Add readonly to --mount or :ro to -v when the container should only read the data.
interview.followUp: Can multiple containers share one volume with different access modes? Yes. Some can mount it read-write while others mount it read-only.

keyPoints: Use docker volume subcommands to create, inspect, list, remove, or prune volumes.
Volumes store container data independently from the container that uses them.
Docker stores a volume in a host directory, but Docker manages that storage.
Use volumes when container data must persist.
Volumes can be managed with Docker CLI commands or the Docker API.
Several containers can mount the same volume, with each mount having its own access mode.
gotchas: Removing a container does not remove its volume. Remove the volume separately when it is no longer needed.
A volume subdirectory must already exist before you use it with volume-subpath.

ENTRYPOINT.summary: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable that starts when a container runs. The exec form accepts runtime arguments and works with CMD for default arguments.
ENTRYPOINT.explanation: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable that starts when a container runs. The exec form passes runtime arguments to that executable, while CMD can provide default arguments. The exec form does not start a shell, so the executable can become PID 1 and receive container signals directly.

parameters.name: arguments
parameters.description: The executable and optional fixed arguments, written as a JSON array or shell command.

ENTRYPOINT.returns: A container startup configuration that defines the executable and its default arguments.

example.title: A simple web image
example.code:
FROM nginx:alpine

COPY index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
EXPOSE 80
ENTRYPOINT ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]
example.explanation: This image uses Nginx as its main process. It copies a web page into the image and documents port 80.

useCases.title: Set the main program
useCases.scenario: An image should behave like one command-line program.

useCases.title: Combine with CMD
useCases.scenario: The image needs stable startup arguments plus user-changeable defaults.

useCases.title: Run as PID 1
useCases.scenario: A program must receive stop and other Unix signals.

useCases.title: Override at runtime
useCases.scenario: A one-off container needs a different startup executable.

interview.question: How do ENTRYPOINT, CMD, and docker run arguments work together?
interview.answer: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that starts the container. With exec form, arguments given to docker run are added after the ENTRYPOINT arguments, and they replace CMD arguments.
interview.followUp: What happens with shell-form ENTRYPOINT? It runs through /bin/sh -c, ignores CMD and docker run arguments, and does not make the executable PID 1.

interview.question: What is the usual way to combine ENTRYPOINT and CMD?
interview.answer: Use exec-form ENTRYPOINT for the stable command and exec-form CMD for default arguments. A user can replace those default CMD arguments by passing arguments to docker run.
interview.followUp: Why must CMD also use exec form here? Shell-form CMD is wrapped in /bin/sh -c, so ENTRYPOINT receives a shell command instead of the intended argument list.

interview.question: Why is exec-form ENTRYPOINT preferred for long-running programs?
interview.answer: The exec form does not invoke a command shell automatically. This avoids shell processing and lets the executable run as the container's PID 1, so it can receive Unix signals.
interview.followUp: How can a shell-form entrypoint improve signal handling? Start the long-running command with exec so it replaces the shell process.

keyPoints: Use ENTRYPOINT to make the image start as a particular executable.
Runtime arguments are added after the executable and its fixed arguments in exec form.
Use docker run --entrypoint to replace the configured executable for one container.
Shell form is easier to write, but it changes argument handling and process behavior.
Shell-form ENTRYPOINT can expand environment variables through the command shell.
gotchas: Do not use the shell form when the image must accept CMD defaults or arguments from docker run.
If a Dockerfile has several ENTRYPOINT instructions, Docker uses only the final one.
Write exec-form arguments as valid JSON arrays with double quotes, not single quotes.

ENV.summary: A Docker Compose service defines how to create and run one kind of container. Services are declared under the required top-level services map and can configure images, builds, ports, environment variables, dependencies, and storage.
ENV.explanation: A Compose service describes containers that share the same image and runtime settings. Put services under the required top-level services map. A service can use an existing image or build one from source, then configure ports, environment variables, files, dependencies, and other container settings.
ENV.syntax:
services:
  SERVICE_NAME:
    image: IMAGE
    # other service options

parameters.name: services
parameters.description: Map of service names to service definitions.

parameters.name: image
parameters.description: Container image to run for the service.

parameters.name: build
parameters.description: Instructions for building the service image from source.

parameters.name: environment
parameters.description: Environment variables for service containers.

parameters.name: env_file
parameters.description: Files containing environment variables to load.

parameters.name: ports
parameters.description: Container ports to publish on the host.

parameters.name: expose
parameters.description: Internal container ports available to other services.

example.title: A basic Compose service
example.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:latest
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    environment:
      APP_MODE: "demo"
example.explanation: This defines one service named web. Compose starts it from the nginx image, publishes port 80 as port 8080 on the host, and sets an environment variable.

useCases.title: Multi-service applications
useCases.scenario: Define a web server and database as separate containers in one application.

useCases.title: Runtime configuration
useCases.scenario: Set different ports and environment variables for each container.

useCases.title: Local image builds
useCases.scenario: Build an application image from a local Dockerfile.

useCases.title: Configuration and storage
useCases.scenario: Share configuration files or data with service containers.

interview.question: What is a service in Docker Compose?
interview.answer: A service is a Compose definition for a set of similar containers. All containers in that service are created with the same image and runtime arguments.
interview.followUp: How does a service differ from a container? A service is the declarative configuration and scaling unit; containers are the running instances created from it.

interview.question: How is a Compose service declared?
interview.answer: The services top-level key is a map. Each key is a service name, and each value contains the configuration applied to that service's containers.
interview.followUp: What happens if a service has build but no image? Compose can build the image from the build configuration and use it for the service.

interview.question: How does Compose set service environment variables?
interview.answer: Use environment to set variables directly in a service. Use env_file to load variables from files. If both are present, environment values override env_file values.
interview.followUp: How are multiple env_file entries handled? They are read from top to bottom, and the last value for a repeated variable wins.

keyPoints: Every Compose file needs a top-level services map.
Each map key names one service.
build describes how Compose creates the service image from source.
Logs are collected by default. Set attach to false to stop automatic log collection until requested.
env_file loads variables from one or more files.
Direct environment settings override values loaded from env_file.
expose makes internal container ports available to linked services without publishing them to the host.
gotchas: expose makes container ports available to other services, but it does not publish them on the host. Use ports when host access is needed.

environment.sourceTitle: Set environment variables within your container's environment
environment.summary: Set variables in Compose with `environment`, or load them from files with `env_file`. Use `docker compose run -e` for a temporary value on one command.
environment.explanation: Use the Compose `environment` attribute to add variables to a container. Mapping syntax sets an explicit value. List syntax with only a variable name takes that value from the shell. You can also use `env_file` for variables stored in a separate file.
environment.syntax:
services:
  <service>:
    environment:
      NAME: value
    env_file: path/to/file.env

parameters.name: services.<service>.environment
parameters.description: Compose service name and its environment settings.

parameters.name: services.<service>.env_file
parameters.description: One or more files containing service environment variables.

environment.returns: The configured variables become part of the service container's environment.

example.title: Set container variables with Compose
example.code:
services:
  webapp:
    image: nginx
    environment:
      DEBUG: "true"
      LOG_LEVEL:
example.explanation: This Compose service sets DEBUG directly and takes LOG_LEVEL from the shell environment.
