useCases.scenario: A service needs fixed settings such as a debug switch or log level.

useCases.title: Reuse an environment file
useCases.scenario: Several services share variables kept in a separate file.

useCases.title: Override a run
useCases.scenario: A one-off task needs a variable without changing the Compose file.

interview.question: How do you set environment variables in Compose?
interview.answer: The `environment` attribute defines variables inside a service container. Mapping syntax uses entries such as `DEBUG: "true"`; list syntax can use `DEBUG=true` or only `DEBUG` to read from the shell.
interview.followUp: How can a service read variables from a separate file? Use `env_file`, whose paths are relative to the Compose file.

interview.question: How does `env_file` work?
interview.answer: Use `env_file` to load variables from one or more files. Multiple files are processed in order, and later files can replace values from earlier files.
interview.followUp: Can a missing file be allowed? Yes. Set `required: false` for that file; Compose then ignores it when it is absent.

interview.question: How can you set a variable for one Compose command?
interview.answer: Use `docker compose run -e NAME=value SERVICE COMMAND` for a temporary variable on a one-off command. The short form is `-e`; omitting the value reads it from the shell or environment files.
interview.followUp: When should secrets be used instead? Use secrets for sensitive data such as passwords, rather than environment variables.

keyPoints: Add variables directly with the service's `environment` attribute.
Compose accepts both mapping syntax and list syntax.
Interpolation can fill values from the shell or an `.env` file, and Compose warns when the variable is missing.
Paths in `env_file` are resolved relative to the location of `compose.yaml`.
When several environment files are listed, later files can override earlier values.
gotchas: Do not put passwords or other secrets in environment variables. Use Compose secrets instead.
A variable without a value is read from the shell that runs Compose.
Interpolation in `.env` files does not work with `docker run --env-file`.

EXPOSE.summary: `docker run` creates and starts a container from an image. Options can publish ports, replace image defaults, and configure the container at startup.
EXPOSE.explanation: The `docker run` command creates and starts a container from an image. Options can change its name, ports, entrypoint, environment, and other runtime settings; a command after the image can replace the image's default command.

parameters.name: OPTIONS
parameters.description: Optional flags that configure the container at runtime.

parameters.name: IMAGE[:TAG|@DIGEST]
parameters.description: The image name, optional tag, or digest used to create the container.

parameters.name: COMMAND [ARG...]
parameters.description: Optional command and arguments run in the container.

EXPOSE.returns: Starts a container and prints its output unless detached mode is used.

example.title: Run a web container
example.code: docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:latest
example.explanation: This starts an Nginx container in the background, names it web, and maps host port 8080 to container port 80.

useCases.title: Run a specific image
useCases.scenario: Start an application from a chosen image version.

useCases.title: Publish ports
useCases.scenario: Make a service inside the container reachable from the host.

useCases.title: Run in the background
useCases.scenario: Start a service without keeping the terminal attached.

useCases.title: Override the entrypoint
useCases.scenario: Replace an image's normal startup executable for debugging.

interview.question: What is the syntax of `docker run`, and how does it handle default commands?
interview.answer: The general form is `docker run [OPTIONS] IMAGE[:TAG|@DIGEST] [COMMAND] [ARG...]`. The image is required, while the command and arguments are optional. A supplied command replaces the image's default `CMD`; with an entrypoint, it becomes arguments to that entrypoint.
interview.followUp: How can the image entrypoint be replaced? Use `--entrypoint` with the executable path. An empty value resets the entrypoint, but also clears the image's default command.

interview.question: How do you make a container port reachable from the host?
interview.answer: Use `-p` or `--publish` to map a host port to a container port, such as `-p 8080:80`. The two numbers can differ. Use `-P` to publish all ports declared with `EXPOSE` or `--expose` to random host ports.
interview.followUp: How can you find the resulting host-to-container mapping? Run `docker port` for the container.

interview.question: What is an image reference?
interview.answer: An image tag identifies an image version, and it defaults to `latest` when omitted. For example, `ubuntu:24.04` selects the Ubuntu 24.04 tag. An image can also be referenced by a digest.
interview.followUp: Why might a digest be useful? It identifies a specific image content rather than relying on a movable tag.

keyPoints: Use `docker run`, options, an image reference, and optionally a command with arguments.
Tags select image versions. An omitted tag uses `latest`.
`-P` publishes every port declared by the image or by `--expose` and assigns random host ports.
`-p` lets you choose the host port and the container port, or map port ranges.
The host and container port numbers may differ, so clients can use a different port from the service.
Linux containers receive Docker-set variables such as `HOME` and `HOSTNAME`; Windows containers do not receive these automatic variables.
gotchas: A container port is not reachable from the host unless you publish it with `-p` or `-P`.
Using `--entrypoint` also removes the image's default `CMD`.

FROM.summary: Docker Compose defines and runs multi-container applications from a YAML file. It manages services, networks, volumes, builds, startup, logs, and commands as one application stack.
FROM.explanation: Compose reads a YAML file that describes application services and their supporting resources. It can build or pull images, create the services, and control them together. Commands also let you inspect the resolved configuration, view logs, execute commands in running containers, and manage the application lifecycle.
FROM.syntax:
docker compose up [OPTIONS]
docker compose config
docker compose logs -f [SERVICE...]
docker compose exec SERVICE COMMAND [ARG...]

example.title: A Compose application with a health check
example.code:
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8000:5000"
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
  redis:
    image: redis:alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
volumes:
  redis-data:
example.explanation: This file builds a web service, starts Redis, waits for Redis to become healthy, and maps host port 8000 to container port 5000.

useCases.title: Run a multi-container application
useCases.scenario: Describe a web application and its database or cache in one project file.

useCases.title: Control service startup
useCases.scenario: Use health checks and dependency conditions so a service starts after its dependency is ready.

useCases.title: Persist application data
useCases.scenario: Store service data outside a container so it remains after containers are replaced.

useCases.title: Debug a running stack
useCases.scenario: Inspect configuration, follow logs, or run diagnostic commands without stopping the stack.

interview.question: What problem does Docker Compose solve?
interview.answer: Compose uses a YAML file to define services and related resources. One docker compose up command can build or pull images and start all configured services.
interview.followUp: How can you confirm the final settings before starting? Run docker compose config to view variable substitution and the merged, resolved configuration.

interview.question: How do build, image, and ports work in a Compose file?
interview.answer: A service can use build: . to build from the Dockerfile in the current directory, or image: to use an existing image. The ports mapping connects a host port to a container port.
interview.followUp: How would you make startup depend on Redis readiness? Add a Redis healthcheck and set the web service dependency condition to service_healthy.

interview.question: Which commands help inspect and debug a running stack?
interview.answer: docker compose exec runs a command inside an already-running container and does not create another container. docker compose logs -f follows live logs, while docker compose down removes the application containers.
interview.followUp: How can data survive container replacement? Mount a named volume, such as redis-data:/data, and declare that volume at the top level.

keyPoints: A Compose file can describe services, networks, and volumes together.
docker compose up creates and starts the services defined by the Compose file.
A .env file can provide values that Compose substitutes into the YAML configuration.
docker compose config checks the resolved configuration without starting containers.
Use docker compose exec for commands and live debugging inside an existing container.
docker compose logs -f continuously displays service logs until log following is stopped.
gotchas: The build file must be named Dockerfile without an extension.
Data in a container's writable layer is lost when docker compose down removes the container; use a named volume for persistent data.
Starting dependent services at the same time can cause connection failures; use a health check and a service_healthy dependency condition.

healthcheck.summary: HEALTHCHECK tells Docker how to test whether a container is working. Docker tracks starting, healthy, and unhealthy states from the command's results.
healthcheck.explanation: HEALTHCHECK defines a command that Docker runs inside a container to test whether the application still works. The container starts with a starting status, becomes healthy after a successful check, and becomes unhealthy after the configured number of consecutive failures. Use HEALTHCHECK NONE to disable an inherited check.

parameters.name: --interval
parameters.description: Time between regular health checks. Default: 30 seconds.

parameters.name: --timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time allowed for one check. Default: 30 seconds.

parameters.name: --start-period
parameters.description: Initialization period during which probe failures are not counted. Default: 0 seconds.

parameters.name: --start-interval
parameters.description: Time between checks during initialization. Default: 5 seconds.

parameters.name: --retries
parameters.description: Consecutive failures required for unhealthy status. Default: 3.

healthcheck.returns: The health status is starting, healthy, or unhealthy. The command uses exit code 0 for success, 1 for failure, and 2 is reserved.

example.title: Add a container health check
example.code: HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1
example.explanation: Docker runs this command to test the service. A successful command means the container is healthy. Three failures in a row make it unhealthy.

useCases.title: Detect a stuck service
useCases.scenario: A web server process is running but no longer accepts new connections.

useCases.title: Allow startup time
useCases.scenario: An application needs time to start before probes should count.

useCases.title: Disable an inherited check
useCases.scenario: A base image defines a check that does not fit the application.

interview.question: How does HEALTHCHECK determine container health?
interview.answer: HEALTHCHECK runs a command inside the container and uses its exit status. Exit code 0 means healthy, 1 means unhealthy, and 2 is reserved.
interview.followUp: What happens after repeated failures? After the configured retries count of consecutive failures, Docker marks the container unhealthy.

interview.question: What HEALTHCHECK options can you configure?
interview.answer: The default interval is 30 seconds, timeout is 30 seconds, start period is 0 seconds, start interval is 5 seconds, and retries is 3. During the start period, checks use start-interval and failures do not count until the container has successfully started.
interview.followUp: Why use a start period? It gives an application time to initialize without early probe failures consuming its retry allowance.

interview.question: How can an inherited health check be disabled?
interview.answer: HEALTHCHECK NONE disables a health check inherited from the base image. A normal HEALTHCHECK adds health status in addition to the container's normal status.
interview.followUp: How can Compose use this status? A Compose dependency with service_healthy waits for the dependency's health check to pass before starting the dependent service.

keyPoints: Use HEALTHCHECK to test whether the application inside a running container still works.
The first check runs after interval, and later checks run interval seconds after the previous check finishes.
While the start period is active, Docker uses start-interval instead of interval.
Docker marks the container unhealthy only after retries consecutive failures.
A health_status event is emitted whenever the health state changes.
gotchas: If one check runs longer than timeout, Docker stops the check process with SIGKILL.
Do not use exit code 2 for the health command because Docker reserves it.
Keep diagnostic output short because Docker stores only the first 4096 bytes.

HEALTHCHECK.summary: HEALTHCHECK tells Docker how to test whether a container is still working. Docker reports starting, healthy, or unhealthy based on the command result and consecutive failures.
HEALTHCHECK.explanation: HEALTHCHECK defines a command that Docker runs inside a container to test whether the application still works. The container starts with a starting status, becomes healthy after a successful check, and becomes unhealthy after the configured number of consecutive failures. Use HEALTHCHECK NONE to disable an inherited check.

parameters.name: --interval
parameters.description: Time between checks after startup and after each completed check.

parameters.name: --timeout
parameters.description: Maximum time allowed for one check.

parameters.name: --start-period
parameters.description: Startup time during which failures are not counted.

parameters.name: --start-interval
parameters.description: Time between checks during the startup period.

parameters.name: --retries
parameters.description: Consecutive failures required before the container is unhealthy.

HEALTHCHECK.returns: The container receives a health status: starting, healthy, or unhealthy.

example.title: Add a container health check
example.code:
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s \
  CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1
example.explanation: This checks the local web server and marks the container unhealthy when the command fails.

useCases.title: Detect a stuck service
useCases.scenario: A web server process is running but no longer accepts requests.

useCases.title: Allow startup time
useCases.scenario: An application needs time to initialize before failures count.

useCases.title: Disable an inherited check
useCases.scenario: A base image supplies a check that does not fit the application.

interview.question: What does HEALTHCHECK do?
interview.answer: HEALTHCHECK runs a command inside the container to test its health. A successful command uses exit code 0; exit code 1 means unhealthy.
interview.followUp: What happens after repeated failures? After the configured retries count of consecutive failures, Docker marks the container unhealthy.

interview.question: What do the HEALTHCHECK options control?
interview.answer: The interval controls when checks run, timeout limits each check, start-period gives the application startup time, start-interval controls checks during startup, and retries sets the required consecutive failures.
interview.followUp: Which failures count during start-period? Failures during that period do not count, unless a check succeeds first and the container is then considered started.

interview.question: How can an inherited health check be disabled?
interview.answer: HEALTHCHECK NONE disables a health check inherited from the base image. A Dockerfile can have only one effective health check; later definitions override an inherited one.
interview.followUp: How can Compose change the check? Compose can override the healthcheck values configured by the service image.

keyPoints: Use HEALTHCHECK to test whether the application inside a running container still works.
The command form is HEALTHCHECK followed by optional settings and CMD.
Use HEALTHCHECK NONE to turn off a health check inherited from the base image.
The command result determines health: 0 means healthy, 1 means unhealthy, and 2 is reserved.
The first check runs after interval, then later checks run after each earlier check finishes.
During startup, checks use start-interval instead of interval.
gotchas: A check that runs longer than timeout fails, and Docker stops the check process with SIGKILL.
The check command must not use exit code 2 because Docker reserves it.
Keep diagnostic output short because Docker stores only the first 4096 bytes.

Image.summary: Docker Compose uses a YAML file to define services and their resources. The Compose CLI creates and starts the application from that file.
Image.explanation: Compose uses a YAML file to describe an application made of services. Services can connect through networks, keep data in volumes, and receive files through configs or secrets. The Compose CLI creates and starts these resources from the file.
Image.syntax:
docker compose up

docker compose ps

example.title: A small Compose application
example.code:
services:
  web:
    image: nginx:alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

volumes:
  db-data: {}
example.explanation: This file defines two services. Compose starts their containers, creates the volume, and publishes the web service on port 8080.

useCases.scenario: Run a web application and database together from one YAML file.

useCases.title: Persist service data
useCases.scenario: Keep database files after a container is replaced.

useCases.title: Control service communication
useCases.scenario: Connect only selected services on an isolated network.

useCases.title: Supply secrets and configuration
useCases.scenario: Provide certificates or runtime settings as mounted files.

interview.question: What is a Compose file used for?
interview.answer: A Compose file is a YAML file that describes a multi-container application. It defines services and can also define networks, volumes, configs, and secrets.
interview.followUp: How do services communicate? They communicate through networks that provide routes between connected containers.

interview.question: What does `docker compose up` do?
interview.answer: `docker compose up` starts the services in the configuration. It also creates needed networks and volumes and injects declared configs and secrets.
interview.followUp: What command shows the current service state? `docker compose ps` shows containers, status, and published ports.

interview.question: What is a Docker image?
interview.answer: An image is an immutable package containing the files, binaries, libraries, and configuration needed to run a container. Images are built from layers, with each layer representing filesystem changes.
interview.followUp: How can you inspect those layers? Use `docker image history IMAGE`, and add `--no-trunc` when full commands are needed.

keyPoints: A service represents an application component and runs one or more containers from the same image and configuration.
Networks let containers in connected services communicate with one another.
Volumes provide persistent filesystem mounts for service data.
Secrets are for sensitive configuration and are mounted as files inside service containers.
A Docker image cannot be changed after creation; changes require a new image or an added layer.
Each image layer records filesystem changes such as adding, removing, or modifying files.
gotchas: A project groups the resources for one deployment. Its name helps isolate those resources from other Compose applications.
The size shown by image listing is not the same as the amount downloaded.
Image history normally shortens long commands. Use `--no-trunc` to display them fully.

Image layer.sourceTitle: How image layers and the build cache work | Docker Learn
Image layer.summary: Docker images are stacks of read-only layers. Docker reuses unchanged layers during builds, while each container adds a separate writable layer for its file changes.
Image layer.explanation: An image is an ordered stack of read-only layers. Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the filesystem adds a layer. A container adds a thin writable layer above them, so file changes stay separate from the image. Docker can reuse unchanged layers from the build cache, and images can share the same base layers.

example.title: List image layers
example.code: docker image history --format 'table {{.CreatedBy}}\t{{.Size}}' todo-app
example.explanation: This lists the image layers from newest to oldest. It shows the instruction that created each layer and its size.

useCases.title: Inspect image contents
useCases.scenario: Inspect why an image is large or which Dockerfile instruction created a large layer.

useCases.title: Reuse base layers
useCases.scenario: Share storage and download data between images that use the same base image.

useCases.title: Speed up rebuilds
useCases.scenario: Keep dependency installation cached while changing application source code.

useCases.title: Persist container data
useCases.scenario: Store application data beyond the lifetime of a container.

interview.question: What is a Docker image layer?
interview.answer: An image is an ordered stack of immutable, read-only filesystem layers. Each layer records additions, changes, or deletions. Docker combines them to present one filesystem to a container.
interview.followUp: What happens when a container changes an image file? The change is written to the container's writable layer, while the original image layer stays unchanged.

interview.question: How does the Docker build cache work?
interview.answer: Docker reuses a cached build step only when the inputs that step depends on have not changed. If an earlier step changes, later dependent steps may need to run again.
interview.followUp: How can a Dockerfile reduce rebuild time? Put stable dependency files and their install step before frequently changing source files.

interview.question: Where do files written by a running container go?
interview.answer: A container gets a thin writable layer above the image's read-only layers. Reads use the highest layer containing a file, and writes go to the writable layer.
interview.followUp: How can container data survive container removal? Store it in a Docker volume or bind mount instead of only in the writable layer.

keyPoints: A layer stores filesystem additions, modifications, or deletions.
Image layers are immutable after creation.
Use docker image history to inspect an image's layers in reverse creation order.
Images based on the same base image can share its layers, which saves storage and download time.
Docker stores completed build steps in a cache and can reuse them in later builds.
Running a container adds a writable layer above the image layers.
gotchas: Data written to a container's writable layer is lost when the container is removed. Use a volume for data that must remain.
Not every Dockerfile instruction adds filesystem data. EXPOSE and CMD set metadata and do not change the filesystem.
FROM starts the image from another image's layers. It does not copy those files into a new layer.

LABEL.summary: Docker labels are string key-value metadata attached to objects such as images, containers, volumes, and networks. Use them to organize objects, store information, and filter or automate Docker resources.
LABEL.explanation: Docker labels are string key-value pairs attached to Docker objects such as images, containers, volumes, and networks. Use them to organize objects, record information, or support automation. Each key is unique within an object, so a later value replaces an earlier value for the same key.
LABEL.syntax:
LABEL key="value"
docker build --label key=value
docker run --label key=value

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: The label key, optionally using a namespace prefix such as `com.example.version`.

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: The label value. Serialize structured data to a string before storing it.

parameters.name: object
parameters.description: A Docker object such as an image, container, volume, network, daemon, Swarm node, or Swarm service.

example.title: Add image labels
example.code:
LABEL com.example.version="1.0"
LABEL com.example.description="Web application"
example.explanation: This Dockerfile adds two metadata labels to the image.
